articles.title: Spanish PM blames Russia, Israel for disinformation in Ceuta migrant crisis
articles.summary: Spain’s Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez said there were signs ⁠Russia and Israel had spread the disinformation that triggered the rush of migrants into Ceuta.
articles.body: Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez said on Monday there were signs ⁠Russia and Israel had spread the disinformation over Spain’s migration policy that triggered last month’s rush of migrants into Ceuta, but no evidence of Moroccan involvement. Over 72,000 migrants irregularly crossed from Morocco into the tiny Spanish territory between July 30 and 31 in an unprecedented surge at one of the European Union’s ⁠only two land borders with Africa, prompting alarm across ​the ⁠bloc. At least 100 people died in the attempt, according to Ceuta’s local authorities. Spanish opposition parties and some human rights groups have accused Rabat of deliberately allowing ⁠the mass crossing, an accusation Morocco has denied. “When people talk and speculate about the participation ​of Moroccan ⁠authorities, I deny this outright,” Sanchez ‌told radio station SER. Videos on Instagram, TikTok and other social media spread misleading claims that migrants reaching Ceuta by sea could remain in Spain, encouraging thousands to attempt the crossing, Spanish ‌authorities have said. Sanchez said research by the E.U.’s diplomatic ‌service EEAS had indicated that Russian and Israeli networks had been behind the spread of disinformation in conjunction with far-right networks. He said it was clear that the two countries had used the crisis to criticize Madrid due to dissatisfaction ⁠with its position on the wars in Ukraine and Gaza, but gave no further details on the evidence he had of their involvement. Israel’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Russia’s Embassy in Spain and the EEAS did not immediately respond to Reuters’ requests for comment. Rising tensions in Cueta Roughly 5,000 migrants, some seeking asylum, have remained in Ceuta since the border rush, triggering near-daily protests from locals against the Spanish government’s handling of the crisis and sporadic attacks against a ‌makeshift migrant camp at El Trampolin beach, according to police reports. Police arrested three Moroccan ​citizens on Sunday for lobbing bottles filled with corrosive liquids against an ‌army patrol in Ceuta, news agency EFE reported, ⁠citing police sources. No one was injured in the attack, the report added. Sanchez also ⁠announced on Monday that the cabinet would deploy an additional €168 million ($195 million) in emergency funds to reactivate Ceuta’s economy, a ‌figure equivalent to 8% of ​the enclave’s gross domestic product, on top ‌of €180 million pledged last week for medium-term recovery ​efforts.

articles.title: 47km, 0 stops & defunct CCTV: Security gaps exposed in Delhi-NCR bus gang rape case
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: A 16-year-old girl who boarded a sleeper bus in Greater Noida on a rainy night, believing it would take her to her cousin’s home in Noida, .
articles.body: NEW DELHI: A 16-year-old girl who boarded a sleeper bus in Greater Noida on a rainy night, believing it would take her to her cousin’s home in Noida, was allegedly gang-raped by its driver and conductor before being abandoned more than 40km away near Kashmere Gate, police said.The two accused have been arrested. The August 4 crime has drawn comparisons with the 2012 Nirbhaya case as the girl was allegedly assaulted inside a moving bus by its driver and conductor.The Class 11 student from Mainpuri had left home after being scolded by her mother and was travelling to Noida Sector 63, where her cousin lives, police said.She mistakenly got off at Pari Chowk in Greater Noida around 9pm amid heavy rain. Realising that she was still around 25km from her destination, she began looking for transport when a bus stopped nearby.Also read: Delhi gangrape on moving bus: Women Commission chairperson says culprits ‘must get punishment’According to police, the conductor told her that the bus was headed towards Sector 63 and would drop her there. The girl trusted him and boarded, news agency PTI reported.The bus, however, was not operating a regular passenger service that night. Investigators and the travel company said it had been taken to a workshop in Surajpur, Greater Noida, for repairs after developing a technical fault.The driver and conductor had picked up the bus from the workshop around 5pm and resumed their journey around 9pm.Bus travelled 47km before girl was abandonedAfter picking up the girl near Pari Chowk, the bus proceeded towards Delhi instead of Sector 63, police said.During the journey to Kashmere Gate, the girl alleged that the conductor made inappropriate advances towards her before he and the driver sexually assaulted her.Police said the two men allegedly threatened to kill her when she resisted.The bus travelled around 47km without stopping before the girl was abandoned near Kashmere Gate, police said. She then took an auto-rickshaw to the police station.DCP (North) Niharika Bhatt said Delhi Police registered the FIR without getting into jurisdictional issues after the girl approached Kashmere Gate police station."On the night of August 4, the victim came to the Kashmere Gate police station and told police that she had been raped on a moving bus in Noida."On being questioned, it was revealed that the girl was travelling from Mainpuri to Sector 63, Noida, to stay at a relative's house."The girl alleged that the assault took place while the bus was travelling from Pari Chowk towards Sector 63. The driver and conductor later took the bus towards Ring Road and abandoned her within the jurisdiction of Kashmere Gate police station."Police got the victim medically examined, which confirmed rape, and registered a case without getting into jurisdictional issues," the DCP said.The girl was produced before the Child Welfare Committee and later handed over to her father following its directions.CCTV trail leads cops to accusedPolice said CCTV footage helped them trace the bus within hours. Driver Kuldeep, 39, and conductor Sandeep, 26, both residents of Kanpur, were arrested from a parking lot in north Delhi’s Timarpur.The bus was seized and the accused underwent potency tests, officials said.Investigators are now retracing the bus’s route to determine how it travelled such a long distance through areas with CCTV cameras, police posts and barricades without being stopped.A police officer, requesting anonymity, said the route largely consisted of the Ring Road and highways where frequent barricading is difficult because of heavy traffic.However, the officer said police were deployed at the Noida-Delhi border points.Police have collected CCTV footage from several locations and are reconstructing the bus’s movements to establish the sequence of events and determine whether it stopped anywhere before the girl was abandoned.Bus was under repair, CCTV not operationalMonu, manager at Vishwanath Travels, said the bus was undergoing renovation when the incident took place and its CCTV cameras were not operational.He said the vehicle had been taken to Surajpur for repairs before it was being moved towards Kashmere Gate for painting.The sleeper berths inside the bus were fitted with company-provided curtains, which police said allegedly helped the accused conceal their activities from people outside.Forensic examination of the bus found strands of the girl’s hair inside the vehicle, police said. Further forensic examination is underway."We didn't know what happened that day... We learned through police afterwards. We have provided all the information we have and are cooperating with the investigation," Monu said.According to the travel company, Kuldeep and Sandeep had been working with Vishwanath Travels for more than two years.Police are verifying whether the two men have any criminal records and examining whether the bus owner or travel company properly vetted their backgrounds before hiring them."Police informed the girl's family about the incident the same night and called them to Delhi. She was handed over to the family after completing the necessary formalities," an officer said.How the case echoes the Nirbhaya crimeThe incident has revived memories of the 2012 Nirbhaya case, in which a 22-year-old physiotherapy intern and her male friend had boarded an off-duty private bus after watching a movie.The woman was tortured and gang-raped inside the bus by six men, including the driver, who also assaulted her male friend before throwing both from the moving vehicle.The 2012 crime triggered nationwide protests and led to the Criminal Law (Amendment) Act, 2013, which significantly changed India’s legal framework governing sexual offences.(With agency inputs)(The victim's identity has not been revealed to protect her privacy as per Supreme court directives on cases related to sexual assault)You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Delhi | Silver Rate in Delhi | Bank Holidays in Delhi | Public Holidays in Delhi | Delhi AQI | Weather in Delhi | Petrol Price in Delhi | Diesel Price in Delhi | CNG Price in Delhi | LPG Price in DelhiStay updated with the latest Delhi news. articles.title: US PrSM missiles in Iran strike killed civilians up to 50 metres away: Report
articles.summary: International News: The US-Israeli war against Iran began on February 28 with strikes across the country, including an attack on the southern Iranian city of Lamerd that .
articles.body: The US-Israeli war against Iran began on February 28 with strikes across the country, including an attack on the southern Iranian city of Lamerd that killed at least 21 civilians, including seven children, according to Iranian officials.An investigation by conflict monitor Airwars, reviewed and independently verified by The Associated Press, suggests that three US-made Precision Strike Missiles (PrSMs) were used in the Lamerd strikes.Airwars found that civilians were killed as far as 50 metres (164 feet) from the missiles' apparent detonation points, while damage extended at least 170 metres (558 feet) in one case.The PrSM is designed to explode in midair and propel tens of thousands of dense tungsten pellets at high speed in all directions. Photos, videos and satellite imagery from the aftermath of the Lamerd strikes, analysed by Airwars and independently verified by AP, show buildings, streets and vehicles heavily pockmarked by a fragmentation pattern that weapons experts said is consistent with the missile's capabilities.The US military has confirmed that it fired PrSMs into Iran but has denied launching any weapons at Lamerd on February 28.Six weapons experts consulted by AP, including two former US military officials, said they believed PrSMs struck Lamerd and considered the use of the missile near civilian areas unlikely to be appropriate.Michael Meier, a former US Army adviser on the laws of war, said it would be difficult to justify using the PrSM against a target in a densely populated area.What is the PrSM?The Precision Strike Missile (PrSM) is the US Army's next-generation, long-range, surface-to-surface precision-strike missile, developed by Lockheed Martin to replace the Army Tactical Missile System (ATACMS).It is designed to attack, neutralise, suppress and destroy targets at ranges of 499 kilometres or more.The missile can be launched from the HIMARS and M270/M270A2 multiple-launch rocket systems. Each launch pod can carry two PrSMs, doubling the missile load compared with ATACMS.The PrSM uses an inertial navigation system with GPS and features an open-systems architecture and modular design, allowing it to be upgraded for future missions.Lockheed Martin describes its baseline warhead as an “enhanced lethality” warhead designed for the PrSM target set.The company says the missile is intended for targets including air-defence systems, missile launchers, command-and-control nodes, troop assembly areas and other high-value targets.

articles.title: War and heat: Why are wheat prices soaring?
articles.summary: Russia and Ukraine have stepped up attacks on their respective grain terminals in the Black Sea.
articles.body:
Wheat prices have risen sharply amid disruptions to Black Sea exports as the Russia-Ukraine war continues and as changing weather patterns cause droughts that have sharply reduced production.

Over the past month, Russia and Ukraine have stepped up attacks on each other’s grain terminals on the Black Sea. With Russia the world’s largest wheat exporter, and Ukraine among the top 10 grain-producing countries, these attacks have taken their toll on global wheat and grain supply.

Chicago wheat futures, the global benchmark for the grain market, hit a three-year high on Friday, before nudging down 0.54 percent on Monday to $7.79 per bushel by 02:00 GMT. Authorities in Russia’s Rostov region called a state of emergency on Friday after announcing that port closures and navigation disruptions in the Sea of Azov and Black Sea basin have led to a pile-up of agricultural products at farms.

Meanwhile, the rising temperatures and lack of rain have threatened to cut this year’s wheat harvest in South Africa’s Swartland, which produces about 20 percent of the country’s wheat.

What impact is the Russia-Ukraine war having on prices?

Over the past month, strikes on ports, vessels and grain facilities amid the Russia-Ukraine conflict have disrupted grain terminals and forced shippers to delay or cancel cargo loadings during the peak export season.

While Russian missile attacks have impacted Ukraine’s grain exports, Ukraine’s drone attacks in the Sea of Azov have also sharply curtailed Russian shipments of both grain and wheat. At the same time, attacks on Russia’s Novorossiysk and Taman ports have increased shipping costs out of its Black Sea ports.

According to Ukraine’s Ministry of Infrastructure, in July, Ukraine suffered 35 Russian attacks on vessels in port, 22 at sea and 67 on port facilities. By comparison, the total number of vessel strikes for the whole of 2025 was just 14.

On Friday, Kyiv’s agricultural minister said recent Russian air attacks have destroyed around 90 percent of retailers’ food logistics. With transport of wheat curtailed, prices have risen, raising fears of food insecurity around the world.

Joe Glauber, a research fellow emeritus in the director general’s office at the International Food Policy Research Institute, said that the issue, therefore, is less the amount of wheat being produced and more about the cost of getting it to buyers and consumers.

“There’s plenty of wheat in Russia and Ukraine, and ultimately that wheat will make it out on to the market. But right now it can’t, or it comes out with a very high cost, and so wheat prices have reflected that,” he told Al Jazeera.

“There’s a lot of wheat in the world…it’s not a question of availability, it’s a question of affordability,” he added.

Egypt, the world’s largest wheat importer, usually spends around $3bn per year on importing wheat. In the first half of 2026, it sourced more than 82 percent of its stock from Russia and Ukraine.

In Asia, second-largest wheat importer Indonesia bought $361m of wheat from Ukraine and $102m from Russia between 2023 and 2024, according to the Observatory of Economic Complexity. Indonesia usually sources between 15 percent and 20 percent of its wheat from the two countries.

An official at Indonesia’s Flour Millers’ Association told Reuters last week that current stocks can meet immediate food-grade wheat requirements. “But we don’t have abundant or excess supply. We have to look at other origins such as Bulgaria, Australia, Romania and Argentina for cargoes that do not get shipped from Russia and Ukraine,” the official said.

Besides the war in Ukraine, droughts and drier weather patterns have taken a toll on wheat production and contributed to rising prices.

According to the United States Department of Agriculture (USDA), as of July 1, the US, also one of the biggest wheat exporters, is forecast to yield “46.7 bushels per acre, down 0.1 bushels from last month and down 8.2 bushels from last year’s average yield of 54.9 bushels per acre”.

“If realised, the United States yield would be the lowest since 2015,” the USDA said.

In a report updated on August 14, the department wrote: “This year’s small crop is a product of long-term decline in US wheat acreage and widespread drought impacts on HRW [Hard Red Winter wheat] production in the Great Plains States. Total wheat supplies are forecast down 13 percent from the previous year, with larger beginning stocks dampening the effect of the smaller crop.”

For Canada, the world’s sixth-largest wheat producer, the USDA’s Foreign Agricultural Service found that for the 2026-2027 production year, total production is forecast to be 34.6 million metric tons (MMT) – also 13 percent lower than the year before – due to reduced planted area and a return to lower-than-average yields.

Amid the heatwaves that have hit European countries over the past three months, wheat production in the bloc has also reduced. According to COCERAL, the European association of trade in cereals, oilseeds, rice, pulses, olive oil, oils and fats, animal feed and agrosupply, the excessive heat is expected to reduce grain crops in 2026 by around 9 million tonnes to 286 million tonnes.

In a report published in July, COCERAL said: “The weather has started to affect corn pollination in the southern half of France and in Hungary. More damage is expected from the forecast heat in other parts of the EU.”

The El Nino weather pattern is also expected to bring drier-than-usual conditions to the Southern Hemisphere this year, with South Africa and Australia expected to experience droughts as a result.

While the Russia-Ukraine war continues, in July 2022, the year the war started, a Black Sea Grain Initiative was brokered to allow for the safe exports of grain, food and fertiliser from Ukrainian ports to stabilise and lower global food prices.

While that agreement held, more than 1,000 ships full of grain and other foodstuffs left Ukraine, according to the EU. However, Russia ended the agreement in July 2023.

The answer to the current crisis is far from easy, experts say.

Bringing prices down now would necessitate a major shift in war strategy by both Russia and Ukraine, while the impact of climate change could be mitigated by governments implementing policies including improving water management on farms through the use of reservoirs to support drought-affected crops and reduce the loss of production.

Moreover, Glauber explained, while alternative routes exist to ship out grain from Russia and Ukraine, they are costly, adding that a return to a possible Black Sea Grain Initiative “would help calm wheat markets a lot”.

One answer may be for other countries to step in.

According to Glauber, during the 2022 global grain price surge, other wheat producing countries such as India exported more to make up for shortages.

“India, for example, had record exports in 2022. It’s probably less likely this year, just because of El Nino and other other factors affecting them, but they could also provide more wheat. I think the world wheat market proved very resilient in 2022, and I expect we’ll see the same in in 2026,” he said.

articles.title: Scotland quarry expansion uncovered a 2,000-year-old woman’s grave; archaeologists were stunned by its carefully built stone walls
articles.summary: UK News: A nearly 2,000-year-old carefully constructed stone-lined burial containing the remains of a woman has been discovered at a quarry in Sutherland, Scot.
articles.body: A nearly 2,000-year-old carefully constructed stone-lined burial containing the remains of a woman has been discovered at a quarry in Sutherland, Scotland, revealing an unexpected glimpse of life and death at that time. Archaeologists from Highland Archaeological Services(HAS) discovered Evelix, near Dornoch, while carrying out work ahead of a planned quarry expansion. The grave was found within an area where evidence of ancient settlement has also been identified, including features that may once have supported timber roundhouses. What caught the archaeologists’ attention was the unusual quality of the stonework. The structure was so neatly built that, at first, the team wondered whether it could have been modern. Instead, the construction style and archaeological evidence pointed towards the Iron Age, with the woman apparently having remained undisturbed for centuries beneath the ground.Discovery of the 2,000-year-old unique burial in ScotlandThe discovery was made during archaeological work connected with the planned expansion of the Evelix quarry near Dornoch. According to the BBC, HAS was working for local quarry firm ‘GF Job’ when archaeologists encountered the stone-lined structure. The location was already considered archaeologically important. The Highland Historic Environment Record shows that the wider Evelix area has produced evidence of prehistoric activity, including burial remains, cremation burials, pottery and features linked to earlier settlement. This newly discovered structure stood out because of its carefully constructed stone lining. Instead of looking like a simple hole dug into the ground, it had been deliberately built with substantial masonry. As per the BBC, archaeologist Lynne McKeggie said the team initially thought the structure might be modern because of how well the stonework had been put together. That first impression quickly changed once the remains and other evidence were examined.What did the Iron Age grave of a woman look likeThe structure was dug into sand and measured approximately 3 metres long, 2 metres wide and 1 metre deep, according to the BBC. A small stone staircase formed part of the construction, adding another feature to the burial. Inside, the remains of an individual were found tucked into one corner. The archaeological team believes the individual was a woman and that she may have lain there undisturbed since the Iron Age. The careful construction is one of the most striking parts of the discovery. The stonework had been fitted together so neatly that the archaeologists described the structure as ‘beautifully made.’ Its appearance raises questions about why so much effort was put into creating it.The Highland Historic Environment Record provides an important background to the discovery. The people who built the structure were working without modern machinery, yet they created a substantial stone-lined space with a staircase. The result survived beneath the landscape for roughly two millennia before quarry-related archaeological work exposed it. Earlier archaeological work at the Evelix quarry area had already shown that the landscape contained evidence of prehistoric activity.Absence of objects in the women’s graveThe burial does not appear to have contained a collection of obvious grave goods. The BBC reported that no objects were found inside the structure, although archaeologists did identify a large quantity of animal bone. The absence of objects does not make the discovery less significant. In fact, it leaves more questions about the purpose of the structure and the circumstances surrounding the woman's burial. The animal remains may provide useful evidence as further analysis takes place. The construction itself can offer clues about the importance of the site to the people who used it. The wider archaeological record for Evelix also shows that prehistoric burials and settlement activity had previously occurred in the area.What can the skeleton reveal about the womanThe remains could eventually provide a much more personal picture of the woman who was buried at the site. BBC reports that GF Job is funding further analysis of the human remains. Specialists will study the skeleton in greater detail, with the aim of learning more about the individual and the circumstances surrounding the burial. For now, many details remain unknown. Her exact age, background and life story cannot be established simply from the discovery itself. Those answers will depend on the scientific examination still to come. Archaeologists are using photographs and 3D scans to preserve information about the structure and the position of the remains.Once the further analysis has been carried out, the skeleton will be made available to Treasure Trove Scotland for potential allocation to a museum. What began as archaeological work ahead of a modern quarry expansion has revealed a carefully constructed resting place that had remained hidden for around 2,000 years. The woman's identity may never be known, but the grave itself has survived as a quiet reminder of the care and effort that people in Iron Age Sutherland could invest in remembering their dead.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Lindsay Clancy defense attorney ‘nervous’ awaiting verdict
articles.summary: Before the jury in Lindsay Clancy’s murder trial began deliberations for the third day, defense attorney Kevin Reddington told reporters at Plymouth Superior Court that he was nervous.
articles.body: Just before the jury in Lindsay Clancy’s murder trial began deliberations for the third day Monday, defense attorney Kevin Reddington told reporters outside Plymouth Superior Court that he was nervous for the outcome. When asked how he was feeling ahead of court, Reddington said he was feeling “typical, nervous.” Reporters later asked Reddington whether Clancy is ready for the trial to be over. “I think everybody is,” he said Monday. He also criticized the media for picking apart Clancy’s case and the symptoms she said she was facing at the time of the killings. “This weekend has been horrific with the coverage,” Reddington said. “And by that I mean (Sean) Hannity, with his men, discussing every little inch of Lindsay’s symptoms and criticizing. Nancy Grace — to coin a phrase, the queen of mean — who misrepresents facts.” “And these things hurt. These things hurt people. If you’re going to be a journalist, do it right,” he said. Monday marked the third day of deliberations for the jury, which must determine whether Clancy is criminally responsible for the killings of her three children Jan. 24, 2023. The panel concluded shortly before 4 p.m. without reaching a verdict. Reddington and prosecutors representing the commonwealth of Massachusetts offered their closing arguments Thursday morning, paving the way for the start of deliberations that afternoon. Friday brought a full day of deliberations that yielded no verdict, but did bring one question. Jurors asked the judge to review pill bottles and a knife that were entered into evidence, Reddington said last week. On Monday, he told reporters that the jury never got to see those pieces of evidence, so he didn’t read much into their request to view it and called the jury “very thorough.” Reddington on Friday said Clancy was “nervous. Sad. Scared.” He did not comment on her state Monday. She was seen in court wearing a dark green, long-sleeved blouse. Her family members were sitting in court behind her as they await the verdict. Clancy, 36, is accused of strangling her three young children — Cora, 5, Dawson, 3, and Callan, 8 months — more than three years ago in the basement of her Duxbury, Massachusetts, home while her then-husband was out running errands. When he returned, he found Clancy on the frozen ground outside their home underneath a second-story window after a suicide attempt that left her paralyzed from the waist down. Her attorneys have argued she was in a state of psychosis and was compelled to act on auditory hallucinations at the time of the killings. The hallucinations, they have said, were a symptom of postpartum psychosis — a severe but rare mental illness that can plague new mothers and cause hallucinations. But the prosecution has said that Clancy was not in psychosis, and that she was aware of her actions at the time of the killings. They have argued that she planned the murders ahead of time and acted with intention, which indicates she was not psychotic at the time. The prosecution has pushed for a first-degree murder conviction. If she is convicted of first-degree murder, she faces life in prison. The jury — comprised of nine women and three men — also has the option to convict Clancy of lesser charges, including second-degree murder and manslaughter. The jurors can also absolve Clancy of the crime, or can deem her not guilty by lack of criminal responsibility — meaning that they believe she did kill the children, but couldn’t control her actions due to being in psychosis. Judge William Sullivan has said that if Clancy is found not guilty by reason of lack of criminal responsibility, the district attorney or another authority will likely petition the court to commit her to a mental health facility. It is unclear what her sentencing will look like if she is convicted of a lesser charge. When asked Monday what he thinks is a just verdict is for his client, he told reporters, “Well, put it this way: If I was representing you, I don’t think I’d be real happy if the jury said you were guilty, right?” The weekslong murder trial is now in its final stages, after jurors and onlookers heard from more than 80 witnesses. When asked Monday is he had any feeling on what was going to happen as he was heading into court, Reddington responded, “Do you think you have any idea who’s going to win the World Series? I have no idea.” Reporters later asked Reddington how much longer he expects the jury to be in deliberations. “If I knew that, I think I’d probably win the lottery, right?” he said. Reddington also said it’s “kind of usual” to be labeled a feminist icon.

articles.title: Trump pushes Apple to change 'Lake Ontario' to 'Lake America' on its maps
articles.summary: The request comes after Google made the switch for US-based users over the weekend. MapQuest, another US map provider, said it will not change the name.
articles.body:
US President Donald Trump has asked tech firm Apple to rename Lake Ontario as Lake America on its Maps platform to comply with his executive order changing the name of the Great Lake, Interior Secretary Doug Burgum has said.

Burgum told Fox Business' Mornings with Maria programme on Monday that "the president has reached out to Apple directly", adding: "I'm sure we may be seeing that change coming up soon."

Google made the switch for its US-based users over the weekend, though users in Canada still see the lake, which borders the province of Ontario and the state of New York, as Lake Ontario.

The BBC has contacted Apple for comment.

Canada installs large Lake Ontario sign in latest jab at US

The renaming has faced pushback in Canada, where one electrical utility company apologised on Sunday for its map displaying the Lake America name.

Hydro One, a utility company based in Toronto, said in a post on X that the name appeared due to their use of a third-party mapping service.

"We are working with our vendor to correct the issue as quickly as possible and restore the proper geographic reference," the company said in its statement. "We regret the error and apologise for any confusion it has caused."

Maps by other Ontario-based agencies also appeared to briefly display the name Lake America, including Hydro Ottawa and the Liquor Board of Ontario.

Trump signed the executive order on Thursday seeking to change the name of Lake Ontario to Lake America, following the collapse of trade negotiations between Canada and the US.

The order directs Burgum to "take all appropriate actions" to rename the lake, including updating the Geographic Names Information System (GNIS), the official US government map database.

Google said in a statement on Saturday that its maps will display the Lake America name for US users to comply with the GNIS.

It added that those in Canada will continue to see Lake Ontario displayed. In the rest of the world, users will see the name displayed as: Lake Ontario (Lake America).

Not all map providers are changing the name. MapQuest, an American free web mapping service launched in 1996, said "we're not changing it" in a short Facebook post on Friday.

The platform also unveiled a tool that allows users to change the lake to any name they choose and share their creations.

After its announcement that it will not be changing the name of Lake Ontario, MapQuest rose to the top of the most-downloaded free applications as of Monday morning on the Apple App Store in Canada.

Ontario Premier Doug Ford unveiled a large sign by the lakeshore on Saturday that read "Lake Ontario Now and Always" in both English and French, Canada's official languages.

"No one's going to call it Lake of America," Ford told American TV host George Stephanopoulos on Sunday. "It's been Lake Ontario for hundreds of years. It's going to continue being Lake Ontario."

The names of four of the Great Lakes - Ontario, Huron, Michigan and Erie - originate from indigenous words.

articles.title: Built in 1928 and bought by a future Dallas mayor, this French-style castle was doubled in size; 98 years later, it’s heading to auction after a $5.8M listing
articles.summary: Real Estate News: After sitting on the market for nearly a year with no buyers, the 1928 French Norman mansion ‘Château des Grotteaux’ is heading for auction. Concierge.
articles.body: After sitting on the market for nearly a year with no buyers, the 1928 French Norman mansion ‘Château des Grotteaux’ is heading for auction. Concierge Auctions will handle the sale, opening bidding on September 16 at around $2 million, according to CandysDirt. This is a significant drop from its initial asking price of almost $5.8 million. The auction of the Dallas property will close on September 29, followed by a live auction in Hong Kong on September 30.Lakewood’s historic mansion to go under the hammerLakewood’s historic mansion Château des Grotteaux first hit the market in October 2025 for nearly $6 million. For months, the seven-bedroom estate at 6941 Gaston Avenue failed to gain traction. So, in February 2026, the listing agent reduced the asking price to $5.8 million and relisted the property. And still, there were no buyers.For a home valued by the Dallas Central Appraisal District at $4.3 million, there were no buyers. Local buyers weren’t enthusiastic about paying the asking price. And now, via the international auction platform, the property can reach buyers across continents who may see potential in what local buyers have passed by. That’s exactly why Concierge Auctions provides hope, as it specialises in luxury properties that defy conventional marketing. Château des Grotteaux is a one-of-a-kind estate with dramatic, castle-like architecture. It is the kind of unique property that fits this market.The former dwellers of the mansionEllen and George Smith are the current owners of the fairy-tale mansion. They purchased the property in July 2020 after the previous owner, Michael Fahey, spent years restoring the grounds. Fahey bought the castle in 2005. After that, he invested a lot in resurrecting the landscape, including the famous secret garden and water features that had fallen into disrepair.The current owners, the Smiths, approached the property differently. They focused on making the house functional for modern living. Fairy-tale castles may be best for fantasy, but that does not necessarily mean they are good to live in. So, they doubled its square footage, adding a primary suite, a completely reimagined kitchen and open-plan living areas. They also added a basement wine room and bar, along with a new garage tucked to the right side of the home. Along with that, they added twin turrets to the existing structure, which enhanced the castle-like aesthetic rather than attempting to restore the French Norman design. The renovations helped make it a modern castle. The exterior also looks different from its original structure.The mansion was originally built by Texas oilman and developer Edwin Cox Sr. Château des Grotteaux translates to ‘House of Caves’. The house was named as a reference to a tunnel that reportedly ran from the property’s southern corner to White Rock Lake. According to local legend, during Prohibition, the passage served as a liquor-smuggling route. The City of Dallas eventually sealed the tunnel, making the legend more mystique than accessible history.In 1929, R.L. Thornton, the businessman and four-term mayor who served as president of the Dallas Chamber of Commerce, purchased the home. He completed the construction and also designed its grounds. For decades, Thornton’s tenure gave the home a Dallas identity.The major challenge for potential buyers isn’t cost alone, but also its architectural coherence. When a historic home is renovated, architects often have a preservation-minded approach. So, the new additions should match the home’s original style rather than look completely different. But the Smith family’s expansion followed a different strategy. They focused on interior functionality and an exterior suited to the fairy-tale fantasy, rather than historical continuity. This means it suited buyers who love the castle look and can afford it without being concerned about its history. Those buyers exist, but they’re uncommon enough that eleven months on the market produced none.Concierge Auctions will hold a live auction in Hong Kong, hoping that overseas wealth may prove more receptive than the Dallas market. Wealthy international buyers sometimes prize uniqueness over local architectural precedent. So, the fantasy castle may really appeal to them.Ready to Make a Smarter Property Decision? articles.title: Putin unleashes new fury on Ukraine as report exposes fear hanging over war’s end
articles.summary: Russia launched nearly 1,500 drones in four days as Volodymyr Zelenskyy says Moscow aims to exhaust Ukraine, with daytime attacks now disrupting Kyiv.
articles.body: Questions over whether the Russia-Ukraine war is entering a new phase are mounting as Kyiv endures repeated drone attacks and near-constant air raid alerts, including growing waves during daylight hours — an expansion beyond the nighttime barrages that have become grimly familiar to residents of the Ukrainian capital. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Russia launched nearly 1,500 drones over four days, more than half of them jet-powered, accusing Moscow of attempting to wear down Ukraine and its population. The attacks have repeatedly interrupted Kyiv’s metro system and daily commutes, Reuters reported Aug. 31, as residents are forced to seek shelter during daytime air raid alerts. As Ukrainians seek some semblance of normalcy at the end of the summer and prepare for the start of the school year, the relentless attacks are again sending already exhausted Kyiv residents underground. RUSSIA UNLEASHES NEARLY 600 MISSILES AND DRONES ON KYIV IN DEADLIEST STRIKE SINCE MAY Russian President Vladimir Putin has simultaneously intensified attacks on Ukraine’s warehouses and logistics network, damaging distribution centers used by major retailers and disrupting food deliveries. Russian drone attacks on Kyiv and the surrounding region stretched into a fifth consecutive day Monday, with strikes damaging warehouses, a retail outlet and residential buildings in the Kyiv region. The attacks are part of a broader campaign against Ukrainian commercial and logistics infrastructure. Reuters reported Aug. 28 that Russia had targeted warehouses belonging to major supermarket chains, Ukraine’s largest private postal company and home-goods retailers. Ukraine’s Agriculture Minister Taras Vysotskyi said that roughly 90% of the food logistics infrastructure operated by retail chains had been destroyed. RUSSIA LAUNCHES BALLISTIC MISSILE ATTACK ON KYIV HOURS AFTER ZELENSKYY WARNS OF MAJOR STRIKE "As of today, roughly speaking, 90% of food logistics operated by retail chains have been destroyed, but that doesn't mean Ukrainians will be left without food," Vysotskyi told reporters in Kyiv, according to Ukrainian state news agency Ukrinform. He said retailers would shift logistics and use alternative methods of delivering food. Ukrainian outlet TSN reported Aug. 30 that some NOVUS locations in Kyiv were short of bread, potatoes, apples and oatmeal, while supermarket chain ATB had introduced limits on how much of certain products customers could purchase. Ukraine, meanwhile, has expanded its own campaign against Russian economic infrastructure. Ukrainian drones have targeted oil facilities as well as warehouses connected to major Russian online retailers, including Wildberries and Ozon. Reuters reported Monday that a logistics hub in Yekaterinburg was also struck by a drone. Retired Air Force Lt. Gen. Richard Newton, a former USAF assistant vice chief of staff, told Fox News Digital that he believes the military momentum has increasingly shifted toward Ukraine, particularly because of Kyiv’s expanding use of long-range drones. ZELENSKYY SAYS PUTIN 'LOST THE INITIATIVE' AS UKRAINE'S TECH INDUSTRY RESHAPES THE WAR "My sense is the momentum has swung in Ukraine's favor over the last year or so," Newton told Fox News Digital. "The Ukrainians have shown tremendous resolve and capability to push back against Russia." Newton pointed particularly to Ukrainian strikes deep inside Russia against "energy production capability, logistics supply chains, and so forth," calling their use of drone warfare "quite remarkable." He cautioned, however, that Ukraine faces a critical vulnerability as Russia intensifies its aerial campaign. "The current challenge facing Ukraine is the shortage of U.S.-made Patriot air defense interceptors," Newton said, noting that the systems are also in heavy demand elsewhere around the world. TRUMP SAYS US WILL LET UKRAINE MAKE PATRIOT MISSILES IN MAJOR POLICY SHIFT The escalation comes amid new reporting about Putin’s calculations over how — or whether — the war can end. The Economist reported Aug. 30, that Putin fears ending the war without Russia achieving even what he considers a minimum objective — control of all of Donbas — could threaten his position and potentially his physical safety. "They will hang me," Putin reportedly told people around him at some point during the war, according to an unnamed insider cited by The Economist. Fox News Digital has not independently verified Putin remarks. The Economist also reported that dissatisfaction with the war is growing among ordinary Russians and that the mood among parts of Russia’s elite is even more pessimistic, with one source arguing that nearly five years consumed by the war represents a failure regardless of its eventual outcome. Newton argued that the intensifying confrontation makes NATO cohesion increasingly important. articles.title: Fog of flood: Nepal’s disaster raises a Himalayan question for China
articles.summary: South Asia News: The August 26 disaster, triggered by a glacier collapse, has killed hundreds of people and left thousands missing, including hundreds of Indians, on N.
articles.body: The August 26 disaster, triggered by a glacier collapse, has killed hundreds of people and left thousands missing, including hundreds of Indians, on Nepal-China border.Catch up quickNepali authorities said on Monday that 903 people had died and 4,247 remained missing, including 933 workers unaccounted for at hydropower project tunnels, according to Reuters.On the Chinese side, authorities in Gyirong County reported 16 dead and 546 missing as of Monday.Moreover, the ministry of external affairs (MEA) informed that 158 Indians have been rescued so far.Why it mattersThe floods have exposed a mismatch at the heart of Nepal-China disaster cooperation: China possesses far greater resources to monitor the Tibetan Plateau, while Nepal remains acutely vulnerable to hazards generated across the mountain system.The disaster is unfolding as two very different stories on two sides of one border. Nepal's death toll and damage estimates have climbed in near-real time with regular updates from government, journalists, and public videos from the disaster zone.China's tally has stayed comparatively low and thin on detail, a pattern that two Nepali officials told Reuters could hamper future disaster preparedness in the region.Nepalese officials say China’s more advanced monitoring capabilities have not translated into the kind of real-time cross-border data system Kathmandu wants as climate change makes the Himalayas increasingly dangerous.The gap is forcing Kathmandu to confront how much of its safety from Himalayan glacial hazards depends on data controlled by a much larger neighbour.Zoom inBeijing disputes the suggestion that it has failed to cooperate and there is evidence China did provide some warnings before the catastrophe.China’s foreign ministry told Reuters the two countries maintain “sound cooperation in the fields of meteorology, water resources and disaster prevention and mitigation”.“China will continue to strongly support Nepal's disaster relief efforts, strengthen cooperation in disaster prevention and mitigation, and safeguard the common interests of the two peoples,” the ministry said.Between the linesThe problem is the type of information being shared.China’s role is about more than missing info. Tibet’s political isolation makes independently assessing risks, casualties and the performance of authorities unusually difficult.The New York Times reported that Chinese authorities have released relatively limited information from Tibet, one of the country’s most tightly controlled regions. According to the NYT report, photographs and videos posted by bystanders and hikers were among material censored on Chinese social-media platforms after the disaster.The BBC similarly reported that footage widely seen outside China was difficult to find on the Chinese internet and that first-hand accounts from survivors in Tibet were scarce. The Guardian reported that international journalists face severe restrictions on travelling independently in Tibet, complicating outside assessment of the devastation.That information environment matters during disasters because Tibet sits upstream of several river systems that ultimately affect hundreds of millions of people across South Asia.It also creates a striking contrast: China’s emergency services possess capabilities that Nepal badly needs - from sophisticated geological monitoring to tunnel-rescue equipment - while the Chinese political system restricts independent access to the very region where much of that expertise is deployed.Chinese state media has attributed the disaster to glacier instability under the long-term effects of global warming, describing such events as an emerging danger on the Tibetan Plateau. Scientists broadly agree that warming is destabilising high-mountain environments, though they caution against attributing one specific glacier collapse to climate change before detailed analysis is complete.What they're sayingDharam Raj Uprety, chief executive of Nepal's National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority, told Bloomberg: "People even didn't get five minutes of lead time." He added that Nepal lacks weather stations in high mountain areas because of the "lack of trans-boundary data seeding mechanisms," calling it one of the country's "biggest challenges."Sauhardra Joshi, a Nepali hydrologist, said Nepal wanted advance notice of glacier activity from China: "if there are early movements of glaciers and early movements around that area, we would want to know a bit early," according to a Reuters report.The Chinese embassy in Nepal said in a statement on X that Beijing has "always made every effort, within the limits of existing technologies, to conduct monitoring, assessment and analysis and have shared important information with the Nepali side in a timely manner".Steve Tsang, director of the China Institute at SOAS University of London, told the Guardian: "Everything about Tibet is seen through the national security prism. And therefore nobody is going to say anything or report anything that has not been cleared from the very top." He said officials on the ground "can't report a higher figure of deaths, even if you have seen more bodies yourself, until the official statement says that the figure has gone up." Of Beijing's muted messaging around its own extensive rescue operation, Tsang said: "The Chinese have missed a trick," adding that "they don't have that confidence. Their instinct is control."What’s nextKathmandu plans to seek a formal data-sharing arrangement with Beijing resembling its existing system with India, including much more frequent information on precipitation and river levels.Nepal cannot monitor the Himalayan cryosphere alone. China cannot insulate Tibet’s environmental risks behind a political frontier. And India and other downstream states face the same expanding climate threat.The harder test will be whether China shares more information before the next wall of ice, rock and water comes down the mountain.(With inputs from the agencies)Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: A New Jersey town agreed to spend $13.4 million to preserve about 50 acres once eyed for dense housing; the first 17 acres have now become public land
articles.summary: US News: Denville Township in Morris County, New Jersey, has completed the purchase of a 17-acre parcel, beginning a $13.4 million land preservation project th.
articles.body: Denville Township in Morris County, New Jersey, has completed the purchase of a 17-acre parcel, beginning a $13.4 million land preservation project that will permanently protect about 50 acres that had once been considered for dense housing development. The first deal secures land at the corner of Diamond Spring Road and Pocono Road, one of the township's main intersections. Under an agreement between township officials and property owner Springpoint Realty, the town plans to complete the purchase of another 33-acre parcel in October 2026. Together, the properties will turn a former private institutional campus into a large area of public parkland, sports facilities and protected open space.Coverage from local broadcaster WRNJ Radio and community news outlet My Paper Online, along with transaction records from the Morris County Board of County Commissioners, describes the project as one of the biggest environmental and historic preservation efforts in Denville's history. The deal also ends earlier plans for high-density housing that emerged after the property was sold by its religious owners in 2022.First parcel secured at major intersectionThe first 17-acre parcel covers the northern part of the historic St. Francis property. Township records show that Mayor Thomas W. Andes and Township Administrator Steven Ward completed the final closing after receiving approval from state and county funding partners. The remaining 33 acres, expected to be acquired in October 2026, contain historic farm barns, existing sports fields and long-running community festival grounds along Pocono Road. Together, the parcels will prevent major commercial or residential development at an important intersection while preserving a large area of open land in the centre of the township.Speaking about the first purchase, Mayor Andes highlighted the importance of the deal for the community in comments reported by WRNJ Radio. "This is truly a once-in-a-generation achievement for our community," Mayor Tom Andes said. "Preserving a property of this size and importance in the center of Denville is an opportunity that may never come again. Thanks to our funding partners and the commitment of Denville residents to open space preservation, this remarkable property will remain a public asset to be enjoyed for generations to come."Andes said the purchase would protect both the area's history and its natural environment. "This acquisition is more than preserving land," Andes said. "It is about preserving Denville's history, protecting our environment, expanding recreational opportunities, and creating a place where future generations can gather, celebrate, and enjoy everything that makes our Township special."Property has deep roots in Morris CountyThe St. Francis property has more than 130 years of cultural and community history in Morris County. Historical information cited by WRNJ Radio and local preservation archives shows that the land was once part of the Glover estate, known as Rockaway Farms. Colonel John Heyward Glover established the estate in the early 1800s along the Rockaway River. During the 19th century, the property became linked to Jeremiah G. Hamilton, a successful Wall Street investor and one of the few African American millionaires of his time. The land was later owned by Louis Fenn Wadsworth, an important figure in early American sports history who is widely regarded as one of the forefathers of organised baseball. In 1895, the northern part of the property was purchased by the Sisters of the Sorrowful Mother. They established the St. Francis Residential Community and health resort. For decades, the property and surrounding fields hosted community events, including annual festivals connected with St. Clare's Hospital. After the campus was sold in 2022, most of the modern institutional buildings were demolished. The original timber barns, open fields, wooded areas and rolling landscape, however, remained.Public funding helps secure the landThe $13.4 million purchase is being paid for through a combination of municipal, county and state funding. The Morris County Office of Planning and Preservation said county commissioners provided a $5.7 million grant through the Morris County Open Space and Farmland Preservation Trust Fund. Additional money came from the New Jersey Green Acres Program, which supports municipal land conservation, and local tax revenue from the voter-approved Denville Open Space and Recreation Trust Fund. After the senior living community closed, private owner Springpoint Realty considered other commercial uses for the property. Changing market conditions and continued interest from township officials eventually helped move the site towards permanent preservation.Springpoint President and Chief Executive Officer Anthony A. Argondizza welcomed the decision. "Denville is a beautiful place, and we appreciate the township's interest in conserving its idyllic setting for the future," said Springpoint President and CEO Anthony A. Argondizza. "The Oaks at Denville will continue the legacy of the Sisters of the Sorrowful Mother and St. Francis Health Resort by providing high quality programs and services to seniors." Argondizza said public ownership would create lasting benefits for the wider community. "The township's thoughtful decision to preserve these properties will contribute to the community's health, providing open space, a park, and recreational fields for generations to come," Argondizza added.Former campus to become parklandTownship officials have developed a broad plan that combines nature conservation with public recreation. According to plans discussed in municipal updates and reported by My Paper Online as part of its coverage of the 2026 State of the Municipality Address, the northern 17-acre parcel will become a public community park. The planned park will include walking paths, quiet seating areas and restored natural habitats. The southern 33-acre parcel along Pocono Road will continue to support local sports programmes. Existing athletic fields will be kept for regional youth leagues that have used them for years. Officials also plan to study ways to stabilise and reuse the historic timber barns. One possible long-term plan is to convert the buildings into a municipal community centre. Environmental studies completed before the purchase also found that the land has important ecological value. Protecting the connected woodland corridor will help safeguard local water resources near the Rockaway River watershed and reduce the stormwater runoff that could come with dense housing development.Part of wider county conservation effortThe purchase adds to Morris County's long-running land preservation programme. Since the county's voter-approved Open Space Trust Fund was established in 1994, the programme has helped municipalities preserve more than 18,440 acres across 39 towns. More than $300 million in taxpayer money has been invested in the effort. Denville was one of the programme's early participants. In 1994, the township used open space funding to preserve the historic Ayres-Knuth Farm. The St. Francis property is now among the largest single open space investments completed in Morris County in recent years. Mayor Andes said the project would help protect the character of Denville for future generations. "This investment protects not only open space, but an important piece of Denville's identity," Andes said. "It is a legacy that today's residents are preserving for tomorrow." With the first 17-acre purchase now complete, township officials are finishing surveys and environmental paperwork needed to close the remaining 33-acre purchase in October 2026.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Notting Hill Carnival revels in 60th anniversary celebrations
articles.summary: Notting Hill Carnival, Europe's biggest street party, has celebrated its 60th year.
articles.body:
Notting Hill Carnival has celebrated its 60th anniversary with three days of revelry fuelled by drummers, dancers and colourful costumes.

Europe's biggest street party continued on Monday with the adults' parade, live bands, more than 30 static sound systems and the scent of jerk chicken floating through the air.

The carnival, which celebrates Caribbean culture and history, was first held in west London in 1966.

"We are the greatest when we come together as people," said Jackie, from Jay Dee's Catering, who has been trading at the event for 15 years with her family business.

The three-day event began with a steelband competition on Saturday, followed by the children's parade and carnival on Sunday.

Across the bank holiday weekend, more than two million people were expected to join in the celebrations, featuring thousands of parade performers in sequins, feathers and bejewelled headpieces.

At 15:00 BST, a 72-second silence was held to remember the 72 people who were killed in the Grenfell Tower fire in June 2017, close to where the carnival is held.

Soca band musician Evan said he would be spending Sunday performing "all of the traditional Calypso and Soca songs".

"Caribbean music is everything," he said.

"It's a culture, it's a lifestyle. How we walk, how we talk, how we smile, how we eat - it's a combination of a lot of things."

Soul-Rebel Marley said performing at this year's carnival was "a blessing", after he played on the Rampage Sound stage on Sunday.

The grandson of Bob Marley said he did not feel pressure from his family's musical history, and instead described it as "a guiding light".

Sophie, Rachel and Sara flew in from the Netherlands to perform in the long-running Mangrove Mas band.

"We took part in the parade in Rotterdam, but now we're ready for the real one," Sophie said.

For Rachel, the carnival is all about "the energy, the colours, the music".

"And, most importantly, the cohesion of all the vibes and cultures coming together," she said.

Patricia said for her, Carnival was about "carrying the ancestral presence".

"A lot of people tend to lose the whole purpose behind the carnival," she said. "A lot of them are more into revelry rather than portraying a theme and enacting something.

"I feel like carrying an ancestral presence, because if they didn't go before me, then I couldn't do this. It's almost like I'm paying tribute to my ancestors."

Tashma, owner of glitter and body art stand Litty Glitty, said that festival adornment was "not just putting on glitter".

"It's deeper than that, and it brings everything to life," she said.

"You find so much glitter in festivals but people forget that costumes like these originated from our culture.

"My mum is from Barbados, my dad is from Jamaica, but we are all one. When we celebrate today, whether it's glitter, your hair, what nails you decide to do - every little detail matters.

"It always goes back to our culture because we want to make sure that people understand and remember that this isn't just a big party; we have history and that's never going to be forgotten."

For many traders, Monday's preparations began early.

Lorraine, from Luv Jerk, said her team began setting up at 02:00 BST in order to prepare for the day ahead.

"It is really hard work but it is really fun," she said.

"This being its 60th year, we're really excited to bring all the energy and the great food and to serve all the lovely customers.

"Ackee and saltfish is my favourite dish but it's also the Jamaican national dish. I just love it, I could eat it for breakfast, lunch and dinner."

Jackie, from Jay Dee's Catering, said this 60th year was also an anniversary for her.

"I've done Carnival for 15 years," she said. "It's very hard. I got three hours' sleep last night and I'm back here again.

"Most of the customers, they come again every year, we see the same faces.

"It's such an exciting time, coming together, seeing all of these lovely costumes and lovely people – we are the greatest when we come together as people and come as one."

Down the street, Christine from Jam Vybz Kitchen was preparing for her first time working at Notting Hill Carnival.

"We have jerk pork, we have rice and peas, we have jerk chicken, curry goat, stewed chicken, fried dumpling and plantain," she said. "We're keeping it simple but authentic Jamaican style.

"As a Jamaican, jerk chicken is one of our main dishes and jerk chicken is what we are proud of. We are proud of knowing how it's done and need to make sure the authenticity of it."

For Lizzy, who has been attending the carnival for years, an early start was necessary in order to find a prime spot for the parade.

"We've been getting old with Notting Hill Carnival," she said.

Reflecting on what the day meant to her, she said: "Carnival is for everybody and it was made to get people to socialise, all different countries.

"All their problems have gone away because they've come to Carnival for a happy day."

Speaking ahead of the weekend, the event's chief executive, Matthew Phillip , said it was "unfair that Carnival is always targeted as a cause" of violence, adding: "It is a victim of crime rather than a perpetrator."

Across the weekend, more than 3,000 stewards were on duty, double the usual number, and more than 7,000 Metropolitan Police officers were deployed to west London.

Ahead of the event, the force said officers would "relentlessly" pursue the "small minority who come intending to do harm", and had banned more than 330 people from attending as part of bail conditions.

The Met Police said 243 people were arrested on Sunday during the first full day of Notting Hill Carnival, for offences including possession of drugs, assaults, sexual offences and possession of weapons.

Two people were treated for non-life-threatening slash wounds from knife assaults.

Last year, the Met made 528 arrests across the two main days of the carnival, including 167 for drug offences, 50 for possession of an offensive weapon, 21 for sexual offences, four for violence with injury and 49 for other violence.

There were two stabbings, neither of which resulted in life-threatening injuries.

In 2024, there were eight stabbings, one of them fatal. Another person was killed in a separate attack .

articles.title: Middlesbrough organised crime probe sees three more arrests
articles.summary: Cleveland Police say the arrests are part of a wider investigation following the fatal A66 crash.
articles.body:
Three more arrests have been made as part of a wider police operation against organised crime, following a head-on car crash that left two police officers and five young people dead.

Two of the arrested men, aged 19 and 24, were held after one vehicle rammed another in Derwentwater Road, between Grangetown and Eston near Middlesbrough, at about 23:00 BST on Sunday, Cleveland Police said.

An 18-year-old man arrested in connection with another suspected motoring offence in the town has now been charged with dangerous driving.

Cleveland Police said a total of 27 people have been arrested since the crash on the A66 on 22 August which killed the two officers and five youths.

The pair arrested following the Derwentwater Road car ramming are being questioned on suspicion of possession of a firearm with intent to cause fear of violence.

The 18-year-old, charged with driving dangerously in Middlesbrough on Saturday, appeared at Teesside Magistrates' Court on Monday and was remanded in custody, police said.

Assistant Chief Constable Wayne Fox said the arrests "would not be the last" as Cleveland Police continued to target crime in the wake of the A66 crash.

PC Tom Clough, 38, and PC Matthew Blades, 37, died when a Volkswagen Passat, which other officers had been pursuing until seconds before, collided with their marked armed response car.

The five occupants of the Passat - all male and aged between 17 and 23 - also died at the scene.

articles.title: 'I wish him nothing but suffering':  Nikitha Godishala's friend knew murder accused Arjun Sharma but didn't think he was capable of this crime
articles.summary: US News: Indian woman Nikitha Godhishala was found dead in an apartment in Columbia on January 3 after a person believed to be her boyfriend, Arjun Sharma, fil.
articles.body: Indian woman Nikitha Godhishala was found dead in an apartment in Columbia on January 3 after a person believed to be her boyfriend, Arjun Sharma, filed a missing person report and told the police that he last saw her on December 31. Hours after filing the complaint, Sharma took a flight to India. When Nikitha's body was found, Sharma emerged as the prime suspect as Nikitha's body was found in Sharma's flat. Eight months later, Sharma was arrested in India and will now be extradited to the US.Reacting to the arrest, Nikitha's friend Jillian Thornton said she knew Sharma and but they could never imagine that he was capable of such crime."Devastating doesn’t even begin to describe the shock, the betrayal, you know, it’s been really hard to come to terms with,” Thornton said. “I wish him nothing but suffering because, God, she just was so good. She was just good in the purest sense of the word, and she was good to him.”According to the friends, Nikitha and Sharma's relationship was complicated and Sharma had "a mean sense of humor" towards Godishala. “Sometimes it felt like he took it too far,” Thornton recalled.Nikitha's family dismissed the claim that Sharma was Nikitha's boyfriend and said that he was a roommate who lost his job and then borrowed money from Nikitha. They said the motive for the crime was financial. WMAR-2 News reported that the claim was not substantiated by local police. The family also said that they found out through media reports that the body was inside a suitcase.“We now respectfully ask the U.S. authorities for transparency, cooperation and answers. We are not asking for special treatment. We are asking for what every parent deserves when their child is killed — the truth,” the family shared in a statement.“They’ve been navigating two governments, two justice systems. They made this happen. It’s not fair that they had to do this,” Thornton said, crediting the family for the arrest.In India, a cheating case was registered against Sharma in April, months after Nikitha's murder, alleging that Sharma cheated Nikitha after taking money from her. The police team from Hyderabad, a city in the south, was sent to Agra, a city in the north after they received information that Sharma was staying there. Since a case was already registered against him in the US and a non-bailable warrant was pending, the central authroities were informed and he was taken into custody.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: India rejects Hague court order to restore Indus waters pact with Pakistan
articles.summary: New Delhi says the Permanent Court of Arbitration has no jurisdiction over its sovereign choice.
articles.body:
India has rejected a ruling by the Permanent Court of Arbitration in The Hague ordering it to uphold the 1960 Indus Waters Treaty with Pakistan, saying the tribunal has no jurisdiction over the matter.

India suspended the treaty in April last year after identifying two of three assailants as Pakistani in an attack that killed 26 people at a Kashmir tourist destination. Pakistan denied any involvement in the attack.

The standoff places the decades-long conflict over Kashmir as the primary trigger behind the collapse of the historic water pact, pushing a framework that had endured three wars past its breaking point. Under the 1960 agreement, these shared river systems feed 80 percent of Pakistan’s agricultural land.

India’s rejection follows the international court’s ruling on Monday that the pact remains fully binding and that India had no justification for ending or suspending it.

The tribunal ordered India to limit construction on the Ratle Hydro-Electric Plant in Kashmir, prohibiting work on the dam wall and power intake structure above certain levels. These restrictions will remain in place until 90 days after a World Bank-appointed neutral expert delivers a decision, expected by July 2027.

The Indian Ministry of External Affairs, however, said the country does not recognise the court and “categorically” rejected the verdict.

India is officially a member of the court.

“This so-called Court of Arbitration has no jurisdiction whatsoever to pronounce on India’s sovereign decisions,” the ministry said in a statement.

“Its pronouncements, now or in the future, will have no effect on India’s actions in connection with the projects being undertaken by India.”

Pakistan welcomed the tribunal’s interim measures and said that its government is carefully considering the details of the decision to determine how it can best assist in finding a pathway back to engagement under the treaty’s binding legal obligations.

Islamabad mounted the legal action after India began work last year to boost reservoir holding capacity at two hydroelectric projects in the Kashmir region. Pakistan viewed the expansion as a first tangible step by India to operate outside agreements covered by the treaty.

articles.title: 13 injured as shuttle bus crashes into barrier at Newark Airport
articles.summary: US News: 13 people were injured after an employee shuttle bus crashed into a concrete barrier at Newark Liberty International Airport early Monday, authorities.
articles.body: 13 people were injured after an employee shuttle bus crashed into a concrete barrier at Newark Liberty International Airport early Monday, authorities said. The injured were taken to a nearby hospital and were reported to have non-life-threatening injuries.The accident took place around 3 am on the Terminal B Departures Level 3 roadway, according to the Port Authority Police Department. A Port Authority spokesperson said the vehicle involved was an employee shuttle bus.Video and photographs from the scene showed the bus with significant damage to its front, including a smashed windshield and damaged passenger door.The vehicle appeared to have struck a concrete wall while exiting the terminal, CBS News reported.Emergency crews responded to the scene and transported 13 people to a local hospital for treatment. Authorities said the injuries were not life-threatening, according to the New York Post.Terminal B roadway temporarily closedThe Level 3 roadway was shut as police and airport crews investigated the crash and cleared debris. The roadway later reopened around 9:30 am, CBS News reported.Passengers using Terminal B were advised to follow airport directions and use the designated lower-level departure area while the roadway was closed.No airport-wide shutdownThe crash did not result in a complete shutdown of Newark Liberty International Airport. Flight operations continued, although passengers using Terminal B could face localised traffic and access disruptions.The cause of the crash was not immediately clear and remained under investigation.Passengers advised to check flight statusTravellers flying from Newark were advised to check directly with their airlines for the latest information on departures, delays or cancellations before heading to the airport.Passengers using Terminal B may also want to allow extra time for drop-offs because of possible congestion around the terminal following the crash.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Trump destroys Kharg Island digitally - with AI slop
articles.summary: US News: The TOI correspondent from Washington: US President Donald Trump appears to have discovered a new battlefield in his increasingly frustrating war with.
articles.body: The TOI correspondent from Washington: US President Donald Trump appears to have discovered a new battlefield in his increasingly frustrating war with Iran: the realm of artificial intelligence (AI), where he can destroy Iranian oil terminals with the stroke of a keyboard, military victories are instant, and inconvenient questions can be edited out.On Sunday night, Trump posted an AI-generated video purporting to show Iran’s strategic Kharg Island being obliterated, declaring that the vital oil hub was being “blown to smithereens.” The video showed spectacular explosions and destruction, which defense analysts say never happened even though fighting resumed Sunday after a month-long lull.There was no Pentagon confirmation as of Monday morning that such an attack on Kharg Island had taken place but that did not stop Trump from declaring a few hours later that “Iran” is a failed nation and the only thing going for it is “fake news from the USA,” which refuses to recognise tremendous American victories.“Iran…IS DEAD! They have no navy, they have no Air Force, they have no currency, they are not paying their soldiers or police, Inflation is at 300 percent, and their leadership is in total disarray and incapable of properly representing the country. The only thing they have is FAKE NEWS from the USA, a willingness to kill their protesters (now over 100,000 people dead. They must be tried for war crimes against humanity!), and a good line of “BULLSHIT.”: Trump raged on his social media platform, inviting ridicule from critics.Iranian officials and much of the US political spectrum treated the presidential outburst as yet another infantile tantrum. “The President of the United States is mentally unwell and has been for quite some time. He fantasized blowing up Iran’s Kharg Island. Except it didn’t happen. And why would trump need to blow it up if, as trump claims, the US has total control of the Straight?” asked California lawmaker Ted Lieu, even as Iran dismissed the U.S claim, saying operations on Kharg were normal.Kharg handles roughly 90 percent of Iran’s crude-oil exports, making it one of Tehran’s most valuable economic and strategic assets. Destroying it would be a major military and economic event – not something normally expected to exist only as a computer-generated video on the president’s social-media account.The episode produced the extraordinary spectacle of an American president announcing a battlefield success while the Pentagon remained unwilling – or unable – to substantiate it. In Washington, the question became less whether Kharg had been “blown to smithereens” than whether the smithereens existed anywhere other than inside a graphics processor unit (gpu).Actual U.S.-Iran fighting resumed Sunday after a month-long lull, with American forces striking Iranian rocket-launching equipment on Larak Island and Iran retaliating with ballistic missiles against U.S. facilities in Jordan; Jordan said eight missiles were intercepted. Tehran also claimed an attack on a U.S. base in the United Arab Emirates, a claim the UAE rejected, saying it had intercepted an Iranian drone over its territorial waters.Tehran, meanwhile, has displayed an inconvenient capacity for remaining operational, with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian attending the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation summit in Kyrgyzstan, where he told Indian PM Narendra Modi that Iran still wanted a negotiated end to the conflict.The contrast between Trump claims and Iranian behavior is becoming one of the strangest features of the six-month conflict: Washington is increasingly talking in the language of total victory while Tehran continues to retaliate militarily, manage diplomacy, contest the Strait of Hormuz and seek economic relationships with China, Russia and other partners despite punishing sanctions.Behind the scenes, the Pentagon has its own problems with reports of dissent among senior commanders over plans to sustain a large U.S. military presence in the Middle East. Several four-star commanders and senior admirals are said to have registered formal “non-concurs” over Defense Secretary Hegseth’s plans. The objections reportedly center on the strain the prolonged Iran operation is placing on American forces and readiness.Hegseth has already presided over an extraordinary turnover of senior military leadership, including the removal of Army Chief of Staff Gen. Randy George. The Army’s senior ranks have been hollowed out by the purge, with some key positions remaining vacant. Reports that Hegseth himself could ultimately be vulnerable to Trump’s famous personnel churn remain unconfirmed. But the possibility is now part of Washington’s think-tank tattle, adding an extraordinary layer of uncertainty to an already unsettled Pentagon.For Trump, AI offers an irresistible solution to all the uncertainty. If reality does not supply enough explosions, victories and surrendering enemies, technology can.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.
