articles.title: Before becoming a major philanthropist, Laurene Powell Jobs spent three years trading fixed-income securities on Wall Street
articles.summary: US News: Before Laurene Powell Jobs became known for philanthropy, education, climate initiatives and media ownership, her professional life began on Wall Stre.
articles.body: Before Laurene Powell Jobs became known for philanthropy, education, climate initiatives and media ownership, her professional life began on Wall Street. After studying at the University of Pennsylvania and the Wharton School, she joined Goldman Sachs, where she spent three years working in fixed-income trading strategy under Jon Corzine. It was a relatively brief chapter, but it gave her experience in financial markets before her career moved in a very different direction. Reportedly, Powell Jobs met Steve Jobs in 1989 while studying for an MBA at Stanford University, and the couple married two years later.Her interest in education and social opportunity also emerged well before Steve Jobs’s death. As reported by Forbes, she co-founded College Track in 1997, helping students from low-income backgrounds prepare for higher education. After inheriting substantial wealth in 2011, she expanded her work through philanthropy, investment and media, eventually building Emerson Collective into the centre of her activities.How Laurene Powell Jobs began her career on Wall Street before philanthropyPowell Jobs's early professional life was rooted in business and finance. She studied at the University of Pennsylvania, attending both the university and its Wharton School, before moving into the financial world.As reported by Bloomberg, at Goldman Sachs, she worked with Jon Corzine, the firm's former co-chairman and co-CEO, in a role focused on fixed-income trading strategy. Fixed-income markets cover investments such as government and corporate bonds, and the work requires close attention to interest rates, market movements and economic conditions.It was not a decades-long banking career. Powell Jobs left Goldman Sachs after three years. By then, however, she had gained experience in an industry built around analysing markets, assessing risk and making decisions with large sums of money at stake. Her professional path would soon move away from Wall Street.How Laurene Powell Jobs met Steve Jobs and entered philanthropyPowell Jobs met Steve Jobs in 1989 while she was studying for an MBA at Stanford University. Jobs had been invited to speak on campus, and the two met during his visit.They married in 1991 in Yosemite National Park and eventually had three children together. Powell Jobs also began developing interests outside the world of finance, including education and social programmes.In 1997, she co-founded College Track, an organisation focused on helping students from low-income backgrounds prepare for and attend college. The project became one of the early examples of her involvement in education and social mobility.Her husband's career, meanwhile, was entering another period of extraordinary growth as Apple expanded into one of the world's most valuable technology companies.How Laurene Powell Jobs built a $10.5 billion fortune after Steve JobsWhen Steve Jobs died from cancer in October 2011, Powell Jobs inherited a substantial fortune. Much of the wealth was connected to holdings in Apple and Walt Disney.The size and composition of those holdings have changed substantially over time. According to Bloomberg's analysis, Powell Jobs's Disney position was once equivalent to about 4% of the company, based on a 2017 Securities and Exchange Commission filing made through family trusts.Her Apple holdings were connected to the shares Steve Jobs held when he died. Bloomberg subsequently assumed that portions of those holdings were sold over the years, with the remaining Apple shares treated as having been sold by 2021.That meant her wealth was no longer simply tied to the rise and fall of Apple's share price. Cash from asset sales, investment returns, dividends, taxes and philanthropic spending became part of the calculation.As of August 31, 2026, Bloomberg's Billionaires Index estimated Powell Jobs's net worth at about $15.5 billion.How Laurene Powell Jobs combined philanthropy with investmentPowell Jobs later established Emerson Collective, an organisation that combines philanthropy with investment and advocacy. Its interests extend across areas including education, climate, health and social justice.The organisation has also put money into journalism and media. Its investments have included publications and media organisations. This marked a significant shift from the conventional model of simply giving money to charities. Emerson Collective has operated through a mixture of investment, philanthropy and support for organisations working in areas Powell Jobs has chosen to prioritise.She has also committed substantial sums directly to charitable causes. Bloomberg reports that more than $2 billion has been donated through Emerson Collective and a Goldman Sachs donor-advised fund.Laurene Powell Jobs put $3 billion into climate philanthropyAccording to AP News, climate has become one of the larger areas of Powell Jobs's philanthropic activity. She created the Waverley Street Foundation and provided it with $3.5 billion in funding. The foundation focuses on climate-related work, adding another substantial arm to the network of organisations backed by Powell Jobs.Her involvement in climate philanthropy sits alongside Emerson Collective's wider investments and charitable projects. Rather than concentrating on one single cause, her activities have spread across environmental issues, education, journalism and social programmes.The scale of the funding has also made her one of the most significant individual figures in American philanthropy.Laurene Powell Jobs has backed education for decadesEducation was not a new interest for Powell Jobs after she inherited her husband's wealth. Her involvement predates that period.College Track, which she co-founded in 1997, works with students from low-income backgrounds. The organisation became part of a longer-running interest in improving access to higher education.As reported by The New York Times, in 2015, she committed $50 million to a project aimed at rethinking high schools. Her education-related work has therefore covered both direct support for students and broader attempts to change how educational institutions operate.How Laurene Powell Jobs became a major media ownerPowell Jobs's financial interests eventually extended beyond philanthropy and into ownership of established media businesses.According to Bloomberg, she became the owner and board chair of The Atlantic, while Emerson Collective also backed other journalism organisations. The investments have placed her in a position where her activities span both charitable work and the commercial media landscape.Her interest in journalism has not been limited to traditional magazine publishing. Her organisation has supported nonprofit news outlets and invested in several media ventures.It is an unusual combination of roles: philanthropist, investor and media owner, with each area connected to the larger network of organisations she has built since leaving her earlier career in finance.How Powell Jobs’s sports investment added another part to her fortunePowell Jobs also entered professional sports ownership through Monumental Sports & Entertainment.The company controls several Washington sports properties, including the NBA's Washington Wizards, the NHL's Washington Capitals and Capital One Arena. Powell Jobs previously held a 20% stake in the organisation.That investment did not remain permanent. Bloomberg reports that she sold her stake in December 2025, when Monumental Sports & Entertainment had an enterprise valuation of $7.2 billion.Laurene Powell Jobs’s journey from Goldman Sachs to Emerson CollectiveThe three years Powell Jobs spent at Goldman Sachs occupy only a small part of her biography, but they provide an early glimpse of a career that began in a very different place.She entered finance after studying business, worked in fixed-income strategy under Corzine and then left Wall Street. Her subsequent life brought marriage, family, education projects and eventually the management of one of America's largest private fortunes.After Steve Jobs's death, that wealth gave her the ability to operate on a much larger scale. She did not simply retain the assets inherited from him. Over the years, she has sold major holdings, invested in companies and media organisations, committed billions to philanthropy and built institutions of her own.Today, the Goldman Sachs chapter is far removed from the centre of her public life. But it was where her professional career began, several years before she became known for the philanthropic and investment organisation that now bears the name Emerson Collective.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: A Kohl’s closed in 2016 and sat vacant for nearly a decade; $28 million later, the 80,000-square-foot store is becoming a church and community venue
articles.summary: US News: A former Kohl's department store that stood empty along Holcomb Bridge Road in Roswell, Georgia, for nearly a decade has been turned into an 80,000-sq.
articles.body: A former Kohl's department store that stood empty along Holcomb Bridge Road in Roswell, Georgia, for nearly a decade has been turned into an 80,000-square-foot church and multi-use event venue after a $28 million redevelopment project. Eagles Nest Church, a non-denominational congregation that operated for more than 14 years without a permanent building, bought the 15-acre retail site in December 2022 for $13 million. The total investment has since grown to about $28 million to strip the old big-box store and rebuild its interior as a modern campus for worship services and community events.According to the Atlanta Journal-Constitution and details from a press release distributed through EIN Presswire, the new facility has an auditorium with seating for more than 1,000 people, dedicated areas for youth education and flexible spaces for different uses. From September 2026, the venue will operate seven days a week and will be available for weddings, graduations, corporate training sessions, conferences and musical performances.Empty retail store gets a new purposeThe large building at 2342 Holcomb Bridge Road originally served local shoppers as a Kohl's store before closing permanently in 2016. For almost 10 years, the 80,000-square-foot building remained empty at the Centennial Village shopping centre. At times, the overgrown parking lot was used by lorry drivers who illegally parked their semi-trailers there. The site's future changed when Eagles Nest Church bought the 15-acre property from New York-based real estate company Rothenberg-Rosenfield through its entity ENA Group LLC. Local outlet Atlanta Daily World reported that the purchase became the first step in a larger 16-acre master plan called The Beacon at East Roswell. The project is being developed with Atlanta real estate firm Regent Partners. The church plans to officially open the new facility on 6 September 2026 with a two-service grand opening called "The CrossOver". Attendees have been encouraged to wear white to mark the occasion.Pastor brings unusual path to ministryEagles Nest Church was founded in 2012 by Senior Pastor Lee Jenkins. A Roswell resident for nearly 25 years, Jenkins also ran for Mayor of Roswell in 2017. His career before ministry was unusual. Jenkins played college football at the University of Tennessee before being drafted by the New York Giants in the NFL. He later spent 25 years on Wall Street as a wealth manager and investment vice-president at companies including Morgan Stanley and Raymond James. Jenkins also managed Grammy Award-winning gospel artists Kirk Franklin and The Winans. In 2009, he wrote a personal finance book published by Moody Publishers. Speaking about the completion of the new facility in a release distributed through EIN Presswire, Jenkins said the project had turned an abandoned commercial property into a place for the community."This project is about taking something that was sitting empty and bringing it back to life with purpose," Jenkins said. "For nearly a decade, this building sat vacant. Today, it stands as a place of worship, community, and connection." Jenkins said having a permanent building would also give the church more opportunities to serve the area. "For years, Eagles Nest Church was a church without walls," Jenkins added. "Now, having a permanent home gives us a greater platform to serve people, strengthen families, and impact our city."Church moves from temporary spaces to permanent homeThe opening of the Holcomb Bridge Road facility ends more than a decade of moving between temporary locations. Atlanta Daily World records show that the church began in 2012, when a small founding group met in a ballroom at a DoubleTree hotel. As the congregation grew, services moved to different locations across North Fulton County. Sunday services were later held in a commercial office park, an indoor entertainment centre at Andretti Karting and Games, and eventually the auditorium and gymnasium at nearby Centennial High School. The purchase of the former Kohl's property gives the church its own worship space while also giving it control of the surrounding commercial land. Future stages of the project, being developed with Regent Partners, are expected to bring Class A retail shops, restaurants, family-focused businesses and a dedicated childcare facility to the wider shopping centre.Former Kohl's becomes an example of adaptive reuseThe conversion of the old Kohl's store reflects a wider trend in American suburbs, where communities and private organisations are finding new uses for large retail buildings left empty as shopping habits change. Turning a big-box store into a church and community facility comes with both challenges and advantages. Architectural plans reviewed during the municipal permit process show that contractors removed the old retail interior almost completely. Commercial display floors and dropped ceilings were replaced with acoustic materials, specialised lighting and stronger structural supports for the 1,000-seat auditorium. The large parking area, originally built to handle busy holiday shopping periods, has also been resurfaced and redesigned to serve church members and people attending events. Commercial real estate records published by Urbanize Atlanta show that the $28 million investment includes the property purchase and the full rebuilding of the structure. It is one of the largest private adaptive reuse projects in East Roswell in recent years.New community venue and future developmentThe church plans to use the building for much more than Sunday services. Leaders want it to become a community hub for local businesses, non-profit organisations and residents throughout the week. The multi-use rooms and banquet halls will be available for public bookings from September 2026. Civic organisations, companies and families will be able to rent the spaces for meetings, training sessions, private events and educational workshops. With the first phase now complete, Eagles Nest Church and Regent Partners are turning to the remaining parts of the 16-acre commercial site. Environmental and site surveys are underway to prepare the nearby retail areas for future tenants. The goal is to create a wider development with shops, restaurants and other businesses surrounding the new church and community venue.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: US singer D4vd's celebrity lawyers withdraw from murder case
articles.summary: The singer, 21, will be now represented by a public defender in the murder trial of 14-year-old Celeste Rivas Hernandez. He has pleaded not guilty.
articles.body:
The celebrity lawyers hired to represent US musician D4vd in his upcoming murder trial have withdrawn from the case.

The star, whose legal name is David Anthony Burke, has been appointed a public defender to mount his defence against the charge of murdering Celeste Rivas Hernandez, 14, whose remains were found in September 2025 in a Tesla registered to his address.

Burke, 21, pleaded not guilty to the murder charges in a Los Angeles court on Monday.

A judge determined last month that he will stand trial for murder . Prosecutors have alleged he stabbed the teen after years of sexual abuse before dismembering her body.

A pre-trial hearing is set for 19 October.

Lawyers Blair Berk, Marilyn Bednarski and Regina Peter said in a statement to the BBC that the court had granted their request to withdraw from the case and had appointed the Los Angeles County Public Defender's Office to represent the singer.

The statement said that D4vd "qualified for appointed counsel".

"We continue to support David and his defence against these serious charges," they said.

"We are grateful that the Los Angeles County Public Defender's Office has taken over the representation and that David has a highly capable and committed team of attorneys and investigators behind him."

Berk, who led the defence team, has previously represented US actor Mel Gibson and film mogul Harvey Weinstein, as well as singer Britney Spears and actress Lindsay Lohan.

Deputy public defender Walid Kandeel said in a statement that Burke was "entitled to a defence that takes his circumstances seriously and carefully examines the evidence".

"We are committed to providing him with that defence," he said.

US singer D4vd to go on trial for murder in death of 14-year-old

Los Angeles County's top prosecutor, Nathan Hochman, said outside the courtroom on Monday that his office was "ready to proceed" with its case against Burke.

He also acknowledged that the singer's change in lawyers could delay proceedings, require additional time to review the evidence, or result in the filing of a motion to dismiss the case.

His team was ready for "zealous representation" by the defence, he said.

Burke had already entered a not guilty plea to charges of first-degree murder, mutilation of human remains and child sexual abuse.

He returned to court on Monday to have the charges against him formally read and re-entered the plea.

The murder charges include special circumstances linked to financial gain that could make Burke potentially liable for the death sentence.

Prosecutors allege Burke killed Hernandez because the teen had threatened to reveal his relationship with a minor and destroy his multi-million dollar music career.

Evidence read in Los Angeles court during the preliminary hearing showed threats she made against him on 22 April 2025, stemming from arguments about his friendship with another girl.

"I swear to GOD I will kill u," one expletive-laden text from Hernandez read, followed by a threat to strangle him and tell her dad lies about him. "i will end ur career and ur life I will damage anything," the text went on.

The following day, Hernandez went to Burke's Hollywood home in an Uber he had sent to pick her up.

Prosecutors alleged that Burke stabbed her once she arrived.

articles.title: Stanley Park body: Police seek help identifying woman
articles.summary: The woman, believed to be in her 70s, was left in a bin bag in Liverpool's Stanley Park, police say.
articles.body:
Detectives have appealed for help identifying a pensioner whose body was found in a bin bag in a park.

The woman, who was white and believed to be in her 70s, was found dead in Stanley Park, Liverpool, shortly before 17:30 BST on Friday. She was wearing a cerise pink Nike t-shirt and was described as about 5ft 2in (1.6m) tall, small build and with strawberry blonde hair.

Det Supt Rachel Wilson from Merseyside Police said it was "a shocking crime" and they believed the woman's body may have been left in the black bag at a walled garden for a number of weeks.

She said a post mortem examination took place on Saturday but the result had been withheld for investigation reasons.

Wilson said: "I want to take the opportunity to ask people to please consider whether you have any neighbours, family members or friends who live in the area, someone you may not have seen or heard from for a few weeks.

"Missing people reports in Merseyside and elsewhere have been checked but, so far, these have not resulted in an identification.

"Sometimes people go missing without those close to them realising, through holidays being planned or simple misunderstandings, and so we may not have received a report of any concerns."

She also appealed for anyone who may have seen or heard anything suspicious in the Anfield area in recent weeks, regardless of whether they reported it or dismissed it as trivial at the time, to come forward.

Assistant Chief Constable Andy Ryan said a mobile police station had been set up in Stanley Park to gather information.

articles.title: Nepal rescuers blast hillside in search of hydropower workers as families wait anxiously
articles.summary: Rescuers have resorted to explosives as they struggle to reach trapped workers, as the flooding death toll reaches 939.
articles.body:
The families of more than 600 workers believed to be trapped in a vast network of mud-filled tunnels along Nepal's Trishuli River are clinging to hope their loved ones can be found alive.

Rescuers continued battling to reach them on Monday, using explosives to blast into the hillside before pumping air into the Trishuli-3A site - fearing a critical window to reach survivors is closing.

"I wish we could find him. I wish he would come home," Anushila Bhandari, wife of Aurus Bhandari, a 33-year-old engineer missing on a project site, told BBC Nepali.

It comes as the death toll from the flood disaster on the Nepal-Tibet border reached 939, according to the country's disaster management authority.

The agency also revised its estimate of the number of missing to 3,925, of whom 592 are foreign nationals.

Roughly one in seven missing people are believed to be workers at the hydropower plants. Nepalese Prime Minister Balendra Shah said on Monday that 279 people had been rescued from the sites.

The rescue operation is being spearheaded by an international team made up of Chinese and Nepalese military personnel, while experts from India, Korea and Australia are also involved.

"I still have a 50% hope that he is alive because there is an oxygen system inside," Sita Pandey, whose husband was working in the plant when the floods hit, told Nepalese daily Kantipur.

Nepal relies heavily on hydropower and has spent years developing the projects along its mountainous river systems. At least 11 projects either completed or under construction were damaged in the floods, authorities said.

Rescuers began pumping air into a tunnel over the weekend, but the families of those trapped say that should have been done earlier.

A team was able to get into a tunnel leading to one hydropower plant earlier on Monday, but withdrew after finding no one there.

"The longer it takes, the more our hope dies. This operation must move much faster because every second is meaningful to us," Jiban Khadka, whose relative is also trapped inside the plant, told Kantipur.

"It's a frustratingly slow operation," Khadka added.

Nepalese leader Shah said rescue operations had been "intensified", noting that 11,379 people had been rescued so far.

Another family member anxiously awaiting news is Priya Kharel, whose brother Milan was working as an engineer in the Upper Trishuli-1 plant when the floods hit.

"Those who returned from the hydropower site said there were people inside the tunnel," she told BBC News Nepali. "So there is hope that if the army reaches them quickly, they can be saved."

Australian engineer Arnold Dix, who has been helping Nepalese authorities with the underground search operations remotely, said rescuers had been struggling to find the tunnels.

"The actual signature of them has gone - everything is just missing. It looks like a lunar landscape," he told BBC Radio 4's World at One.

Once rescuers knew where the power stations were, Dix said they could then decide the best way to access them, which typically involves digging and "blasting boulders".

"There's boulders bigger than houses - I've never seen that before in my life. It's just an extraordinary operation," the former head of the International Tunnelling Association said.

He said he still has some hope for those trapped underground, given the protection the subterranean environment might have offered from the deluge above.

Meanwhile, in Chitwan, a district far downstream from where the floods first hit, makeshift burials were taking place after the Himalayan nation's river systems brought nearly 300 dead bodies to its banks.

The air was thick with the smell of decay, as men wearing white Personal Protective Equipment (PPE) including masks carried unidentified corpses into trucks.

Over the weekend, a large portion of the forest outside the city was dug up. Medical staff and volunteers worked to extract DNA from the unidentified remains.

Ganesh Aryaal, the chief district officer, told BBC Nepali that relatives will still be able to extricate the remains of their loved ones, once they are identified through DNA testing.

"We don't have enough freezers here... We had to choose this last alternative of temporary burial system. We are really overwhelmed," he said.

In Tibet, the official death toll is 16, with 546 reported missing, according to Chinese state media. Footage of the floods has been heavily censored in China.

Chinese authorities have imposed "administrative penalties" – which can range from warnings and fines to short detentions – on people speculating online that the casualty numbers are a lot higher than reported.

In Nepal, authorities have also ordered the removal of online content that they deem to be misinformation about the floods.

Additional reporting by Jugal Purohit in Chitwan and Binita Dahal, BBC Nepali

articles.title: Illinois man missing more than a week as crews scour Great Smoky Mountains National Park
articles.summary: A 57-member team is using drones to search Great Smoky Mountains National Park for Marcin Bachleda-Blaszczak after his car was found at a visitor center.
articles.body: A 57-member search team is combing Great Smoky Mountains National Park for an Illinois man who has been missing for more than a week after his vehicle was found at a popular visitor center. Marcin Bachleda-Blaszczak was last known to be at the Sugarlands Visitor Center parking lot on August 22, 2025, according to the National Park Service (NPS). He was reported missing two days later and his vehicle was then found in the visitor center’s parking lot. Park rangers and volunteers, along with local agencies, have expanded the search in and around the park, looking both on and off trails and using drones to help cover the area, as they look for Bachleda-Blaszczak, according to NPS. 73-YEAR-OLD CAMPER VANISHES OFF THE GRID BEFORE HIS RV TURNS UP IN WILDERNESS Drones are normally prohibited inside Great Smoky Mountains National Park, which straddles the border between North Carolina and Tennessee, but are temporarily being allowed for the search. Bachleda-Blaszczak's family said nothing seemed unusual shortly before he disappeared. "The day before, I believe, was when he had pizza with his dad, you know, chatted with him, said he might pick up a shift the next day at work," his cousin, Corrina Auten, told CBS Chicago. "It was very, you know, like a normal, normal conversation. There wasn't anything strange or amiss," she said. "The next thing we knew, he didn't show up for work and he was missing." URGENT SEARCH UNDERWAY FOR MORE THAN A DOZEN PEOPLE AFTER GRAND CANYON FLASH FLOOD Rangers first searched the area around Sugarlands before widening their search. The team grew to 47 rangers and volunteers by Saturday and 57 by Sunday, according to the NPS. Bachleda-Blaszczak is described as 5 feet, 6 inches tall and approximately 170 pounds, with brown hair and blue eyes. articles.title: Victoria Beckham's company makes its first profit after 18 years
articles.summary: Beckham's fashion and beauty business makes a £7.3m operating profit after years of losses.
articles.body:
Victoria Beckham's fashion and beauty business has made an operating profit for the first time since she founded it in 2008, the company has said.

Victoria Beckham Holdings Ltd, which is led by the former Spice Girl as creative director, made an operating profit of £7.3m in 2025, accounts show, after years of losses.

"We have all worked hard for a long time for this moment of profitability and growth," Lady Beckham told the Financial Times .

"We've been very transparent about the problems that we had in the business but have recovered and are now growing at a sensible pace. After 20 years, people don't look at my brand as a celebrity brand any more."

Last year, a Netflix documentary told the story of her attempting to establish a fashion brand and achieve profitability - and the series itself helped boost sales, "with particularly strong momentum in denim and jersey", according to the accounts.

The fashion side of the company delivered "strong double-digit growth" overall in 2025, they said, while the beauty side, which launched in 2019, "delivered one of its strongest performances to date".

That was led by the popularity of her Foundation Drops, which had a 25,000-strong waiting list and which doubled the size of the skincare part of the company.

The Netflix documentary showed the former pop star talking about her attempts to overcome doubters to be taken seriously as a designer and entrepreneur, then running into financial trouble when the company was "tens of millions in the red".

The business was bailed out by her husband Sir David, who told the programme: "For her to have to come to me and say, 'Can I have some... We need some more money, the business needs more money' - that was hard for both of us because I didn't have the money to keep doing this."

Lady Beckham said: "If he hadn't believed in me I wouldn't still have a business now."

She went on to get £30m investment by selling 30% of the company to NEO Investment Partners in 2017, who launched a restructure.

That included tackling what Beckham admitted was "mindblowing" waste, including "flying chairs from one side of the world to another" and spending what NEO's David Belhassen said was "70,000 a year" on office plants.

In a statement on Monday, Belhassen, who is chairman of Victoria Beckham Holdings, said: "With two complementary growth engines in fashion and beauty, an increasingly international customer base and a focused operating model, the business is powerfully positioned for its next phase of profitable growth."

CEO Sybille Darricarrère Lunel said: "Achieving our first operating profit is a landmark moment for Victoria Beckham and reflects several years of disciplined execution and strategic investment.

"Delivering this result against a more challenging luxury market and macro backdrop makes it an even more significant milestone for the business."

articles.title: Colorado family wakes up to bear eating breakfast in kitchen
articles.summary: Security footage captures a bear raiding a Colorado Springs kitchen, eating Flintstones vitamins and trash before an 8-year-old helped scare it off.
articles.body: A Colorado family woke up one July and found a bear making itself at home and eating breakfast in their kitchen. Security camera footage from inside the Colorado Springs home shows the bear entering the kitchen on July 21 and grabbing a snack. "I was getting ready in the morning and heard a bang. I asked my kids — 8, 6 and 3 years old — if they were all okay, and they were all upstairs playing," Nerissa England told Storyful. GATLINBURG POLICE FREE BLACK BEAR THAT LOCKED ITSELF INSIDE HOTEL BATHROOM IN WILD VIRAL VIDEO "I assumed it was a picture that had fallen off the wall, so my curious 8-year-old daughter, Zara Lee, went downstairs to investigate, and my husband followed to grab coffee," England added. articles.title: Quote of the day by Christopher Reeve: "The fact that I was in a wheelchair and dependent on others for…" - powerful words on disability and identity
articles.summary: US News: Christopher Reeve's words speak to identity, courage and the real difference between physical limitation and personal strength. Best known for playing.
articles.body: Christopher Reeve's words speak to identity, courage and the real difference between physical limitation and personal strength. Best known for playing Superman on screen, Reeve became a wheelchair user in 1995 after a horse-riding accident left him paralysed from the neck down. "The fact that I was in a wheelchair and dependent on others for almost every aspect of my life had not diminished the fact that I was and always would be… their Superman," he wrote. This line comes from his own memoir, Still Me, in a passage describing what happened backstage at the 1996 Academy Awards, where he made a surprise appearance to present an award less than a year after his accident. His understanding of himself, it turns out, was never actually limited to what his body could or could not physically do, and the way he arrived at that realisation, through the reaction of ordinary people working that night, makes the quote considerably richer than it first appears.Quote of the day by Christopher Reeve"The fact that I was in a wheelchair and dependent on others for almost every aspect of my life had not diminished the fact that I was and always would be…their Superman"The real story behind this quote by Christopher ReeveReeve wrote in Still Me about entering the venue that night through garages, kitchens and service corridors, meeting cooks, waiters, chambermaids and maintenance crews along the way. Many told him they were praying for him. Others looked him directly in the eye and said simply, "we love you, Superman. You're our hero." He admitted he could barely believe they meant it at first. Then he realised something that clearly moved him. "They were looking past the chair and honouring me for a role that obviously had real meaning for them," he wrote. "I didn't feel patronised in any way. Clearly a part I had played 20 years before was still valued." That is the genuine context behind today's quote, a specific night, a specific realisation, arrived at through the actual reactions of ordinary people who worked in the building rather than through any grand plan on his part.What the quote by Christopher Reeve genuinely meansReeve is describing the real difference between needing help and actually losing your sense of self. After his accident, he became genuinely dependent on other people for many everyday tasks. That dependence, though, never erased the person he had actually been, or the meaning he still held for his family and for the people who admired him. When he says he would always be "their Superman," he is referring not simply to the fictional character he once portrayed on screen, but to the qualities people had always associated with him, courage, determination and genuine strength of character.Why physical limitations never actually define a personA person's circumstances can change dramatically without changing who they fundamentally are underneath. Someone may lose mobility, a career, or an ability they once took entirely for granted. Those changes can be genuinely profound, and yet they do not erase a person's personality, relationships, knowledge or real contribution to the people around them. Reeve's words are a reminder that dependence was never actually the same thing as weakness. Needing genuine assistance with everyday tasks does not make someone any less valuable as a person.How Christopher Reeve's own life gave new meaning to SupermanReeve became internationally famous for playing Superman in the 1978 film and its sequels. After his 1995 accident left him paralysed, his public life took a genuinely different direction. He became a prominent advocate for people with disabilities and for research into spinal cord injuries, founding what became the Christopher & Dana Reeve Foundation. His experience clearly changed how many people understood the actual man behind the superhero costume. The fictional Superman represented extraordinary physical power. Reeve's later life demonstrated a genuinely different form of strength instead, continuing to work, advocate and contribute despite circumstances he could never simply overcome through effort alone.Why accepting help never actually means giving up your independenceMany people quietly associate independence with doing absolutely everything entirely without assistance. Reeve's quote challenges that idea directly. There are genuine periods in life when people need family, friends, carers or professionals to help them through something. Receiving that support does not make their achievements or their identity any less meaningful. Human beings are, in many real ways, dependent on one another throughout their entire lives regardless of circumstance. True strength can sometimes simply mean accepting real help while continuing to pursue whatever still genuinely matters to you.Why identity can genuinely survive a major life changeA serious accident or life-changing event can alter how someone sees themselves entirely. The person they were before can start to feel genuinely distant from the circumstances they now actually face. Reeve's words suggest that identity can survive even a transformation this profound. His physical circumstances changed completely. His relationships, his values, and his genuine desire to make a difference remained important parts of who he actually was throughout.What "their Superman" genuinely representsThe phrase can be understood as referring to the people who continued to see Reeve for considerably more than his disability. To his family, his friends and the hotel staff who spoke to him that night, he was never simply the man in the wheelchair. He remained someone they genuinely loved, admired and looked up to. The quote therefore also says something real about how other people's perception can actually help preserve a person's own sense of identity during a genuinely difficult period.How to apply Christopher Reeve's lessonDo not define yourself by a single limitation, since a difficult circumstance is only ever one part of your whole identity.Accept genuine help when you actually need it, since depending on others does not eliminate your own personal strength.Remember what you still genuinely have to offer, since your skills, relationships and experience remain real and valuable.Allow your identity to evolve honestly, since life can change considerably without erasing who you fundamentally are.Focus on genuine contribution, since making a real difference has never required perfect circumstances.Look beyond appearances, since a person's physical condition rarely tells you everything about who they actually are.Stay properly connected to the people who genuinely know you, since supportive relationships offer real perspective during major change.Measure real strength differently, since courage can simply mean continuing despite circumstances rather than physically overcoming them.Use difficult experiences constructively, since personal hardship can sometimes create a genuine desire to help other people.Do not confuse real assistance with weakness, since everyone depends on someone else at different points in their life.Why Christopher Reeve's quote remains relevantThe image of Superman is traditionally associated with physical power, total independence and the ability to overcome almost any obstacle imaginable. Reeve's later life offered a genuinely different understanding of what real strength can actually mean. He could no longer do many of the things he once could, and he relied heavily on other people for almost everything. Yet his genuine sense of purpose, and his real ability to influence the people around him, never actually disappeared. That is what makes his words so genuinely powerful. A person's circumstances can change entirely without diminishing their worth, their identity, or their ability to inspire other people. Sometimes real strength was never really about being able to do everything yourself. It is about continuing to genuinely be yourself, and finding a way to make a difference despite everything that has actually changed.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: ‘Let Data Reign’: Trump decries opposition to data centres in US
articles.summary: Despite concerns over electricity and water consumption, US president calls on communities to embrace data centres.
articles.body:
Despite bipartisan pushback against data centres in the United States, President Donald Trump has urged communities across the country to embrace the tech facilities, promising that they would bring jobs.

Trump said on Monday that China is happy with what he called the “anti-Data Center movement”, suggesting that growing disapproval of the centres in the US would divert businesses to the world’s second largest economy.

“The only reason that communities throughout the USA should not want Data Centers is if they want to end up being backwards and poor,” Trump wrote in a social media post.

“If they want to be successful and rich, with far lower taxes and jobs all over the place, let Data Reign.”

As more data centres open across the country, in part to power the growing use of artificial intelligence, the facilities have been met with scepticism – by both Republican and Democratic voters.

Data centres consume an enormous amount of electricity, raising concerns about the effect on the power grid, including possible outages and increased utility bills.

The Trump administration has backed a voluntary pledge by tech companies to entirely cover the price of their energy consumption. But consumer protection advocates have been calling for strict federal regulations around data centres.

Beyond electricity, environmental activists are ringing the alarm over the enormous amounts of water needed to cool down servers at data centres at a time when parts of the country are experiencing droughts.

Some residents living near data centres have also complained of the constant hum they emit.

A Gallup poll conducted in March suggested that 71 percent of Americans oppose establishing AI data centres in their areas.

The issue has gained steam across the political spectrum to the point where some pro-business Republicans are starting to express reservations about data centres.

For example, Republican US Senate candidate Mike Rogers – whose Democratic opponent in Michigan, Abdul El-Sayed , is a vocal critic of data centres – recently backed a one-year pause on data centres in the state.

El-Sayed has dismissed Rogers’s proposal and pushed to link the former Republican congressman to Trump’s all-out support for data centres.

The Democratic candidate has called for an indefinite pause on data centres until federal regulations are in place to require the creation of union jobs, ensure that utility bills do not increase, provide investments in the power grid and protect water resources.

After Trump’s post, Vice President JD Vance on Monday appeared to acknowledge some of the concerns around data centres. He said that while they are an “important part of the AI economy”, tech firms should establish power stations to support the facilities.

“If you build a data centre, you should be putting power back into the grid, not taking it out,” Vance said. “If that is happening, I don’t think data centres are that controversial.”

articles.title: Firecracker factory blast in India kills 8 children
articles.summary: Videos reveal demolished houses and desperate rescue efforts after third such blast at a firecracker factory this year.
articles.body:
Eleven people have been killed as a firecracker factory in India exploded, leaving many injured and destroying several houses.

Three adults and eight children were killed in the accident on Monday. It was the third such blast at an Indian firecracker factory this year.

The youngest child killed was just four years old, according to local police. Several injured people were taken to hospital for treatment.

Videos circulated on social media with images of the scene in the aftermath of the explosion in northern India’s Uttar Pradesh state. The footage showed nearby houses completely demolished at the site of the explosion. Other images showed survivors covered in debris and dust.

Rescue teams used excavators and citizens employed other tools inclWe neuding stones as they searched for survivors under the rubble.

The cause for the explosion was not immediately clear. Local authorities were directed to the scene “to ensure proper treatment for the injured and to reach out to the affected families to provide them every possible assistance”, Uttar Pradesh Chief Minister Yogi Adityanath said on social media.

Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi wrote on social media he is “extremely saddened by the loss of lives”, while also promising compensation for those who lost a family member and for people who got injured.

The firecracker industry in India employs hundreds of thousands of people, and the country is a large global player in this field. Many factories are home-based, unsafe and employ children according to the International Labour Organisation.

articles.title: Fragment of Roman mosaic 'thought lost forever' to go on show
articles.summary: The piece of long-lost 2nd Century Roman mosaic will go on show in Cirencester.
articles.body:
Staff at a museum say they are "delighted" a fragment from a long-lost 2nd Century Roman mosaic of sea creatures that was unearthed 243 years ago has been loaned to them.

The mosaic, which will be on display at Coronium Museum, in Cirencester, Gloucestershire, was discovered under the foundations of nearby Gloucester House, on Dyer Street in 1783.

The original mosaic depicted sea creatures including fish, an eel and a crab, alongside mythological figures including swimming cupids and a sea-leopard.

It was reburied in the 19th Century but years of building construction meant it suffered damage. A surviving section was lifted by specialists and looked after by the Lamplough's of Gloucester House.

Piers Lamplough, son of the owner, contacted the museum earlier in the year to arrange the loan the piece.

He said: "This fragment has travelled an incredible path through nearly two thousand years... [and] quietly connected generations of people.

"We never truly own history. We simply become its custodians for a time, preserving it until it finds its way to the next generation."

The original mosaic was recorded through a detailed drawing by antiquarians Samuel Lysons and Richard Smirke, and the surviving corner fragment was lifted and saved by then assistant curator of the Corinium Museum Stephen Clews, alongside conservator Marilee Parrott.

It was then conserved by Nerina de Silva before remaining with the Lamplough family.

Emma Stuart, director of Corinium Museum, said: "When the mosaic arrived at the museum, we all gathered round in anticipation.

She said: "The museum already displays two mosaics – the Seasons and Hunting Dogs – presumed to be from the same Roman town house that also commissioned the sea life mosaic floor.

"We all thought the mosaic lost forever, so to have a fragment find its way back to us after all this time is incredibly exciting."

Stuart said the piece was "tangible evidence" of the early illustrations and 1980s photographs of yet "another incredible mosaic from Roman Corinium".

"You get a wonderful impression of the colours and materials used when you see it up close," she said.

Dr Pat Witts, from the Association for the Study and Preservation of Roman Mosaics (ASPROM), said the "lost mosaic has been described as one of the best drawn and most classical in style of all the Romano-British mosaics".

"So it is thrilling that part survives and has returned to the museum on loan," she said.

The mosaic is due to be on display at the Corinium Museum by the end of the year.

articles.title: What to know: US court hearing held for alleged Lockerbie bombmaker
articles.summary: Abu Agila Mohammad Mas’ud Kheir Al-Marimi is the third person charged in the downing of Pan Am Flight 103.
articles.body:
A United States judge has scheduled a hearing in Washington, DC, to discuss the case against a former Libyan intelligence official accused of participating in the 1988 Lockerbie bombing, an attack on a commercial aeroplane that killed everyone on board.

The case concerns Abu Agila Mohammad Mas’ud Kheir Al-Marimi, who reportedly worked for Libya’s external security organisation at the time of the bombing.

Federal prosecutors have accused Mas’ud of delivering the bomb that was later loaded onto Pan Am Flight 103, which exploded over Lockerbie, Scotland, on December 21, 1988.

His trial is expected to be the first held in the US for the Lockerbie bombing. Hundreds of people, many of them Americans, were killed in the explosion.

A court hearing is currently scheduled for Tuesday, but the trial has long been delayed.

Jury selection was set to begin last week. But US District Judge Dabney Friedrich unexpectedly postponed the trial, citing the discovery of new evidence. The delay is designed to give Mas’ud’s defence team time to review the new material.

It is yet another stunning development in a saga that has witnessed countless twists and turns. Here’s what you need to know:

The US has accused Mas’ud of making the bomb that downed a Pan American Airways plane bound for New York City.

Just over half an hour after it took off from London’s Heathrow airport, the flight exploded, killing all 259 people on board, including passengers and crew.

The plane was 9.45km (31,000 feet) over Scotland when the bomb went off, and the wreckage tumbled onto the town of Lockerbie, destroying an entire city block and killing 11 people on the ground.

The death toll included citizens of 21 countries, including 190 Americans and 43 from the United Kingdom. The passengers included 35 students from New York’s Syracuse University who were returning from a semester abroad.

Nearly four decades later, the bombing remains the deadliest “terrorist” attack in UK history.

Judge Friedrich did not specify the nature of the newly discovered evidence.

According to The Associated Press news agency, Mas’ud’s lawyers said federal prosecutors disclosed the new evidence to them days before jury selection was scheduled to begin.

They added that “constitutional and ethical obligations require the defense to investigate this development”.

The possible identity of the Lockerbie bombmaker has remained a mystery for years, but US prosecutors have accused Mas’ud of taking part in making and planting the explosive.

Mas’ud, now in his mid-70s, is charged with two counts of destruction of an aircraft resulting in death. He faces a maximum penalty of life in prison if convicted.

He has denied building the bomb and pleaded not guilty to the charges.

US officials charged Mas’ud on December 21, 2020 – nearly 32 years to the day after the bombing. He was arrested two years later.

According to US prosecutors, Mas’ud worked for the Libyan intelligence service from approximately 1973 to 2011, rising to the rank of colonel.

The US government alleges that Mas’ud and others carried out the bombing at the direction of then-Libyan leader Muammar Gaddafi, who was ousted and killed during the country’s civil war in 2011.

Prosecutors say Mas’ud flew from Libya to Malta with a bomb concealed in a Samsonite suitcase. Upon meeting his co-conspirators, he allegedly set the bomb’s timer to go off 11 hours later.

From there, Mas’ud is accused of handing the bomb to a co-conspirator, who placed the suitcase on an airport conveyor belt, before returning to the Libyan capital, Tripoli.

Two other suspected Libyan intelligence agents, Abd al-Basit al-Magrahi and Al-Amin Khalifa Fahimah, were tried by a panel of Scottish judges in the Netherlands in 2000.

The court acquitted Fahimah and convicted al-Magrahi in 2001, sentencing him to life imprisonment.

Al-Magrahi was released on compassionate grounds in 2009 and died in Libya in 2012. Fahimah died on August 25 this year. US prosecutors believe they met Mas’ud in Malta to plant the bomb.

Why has it taken so long for this case to be tried?

The Lockerbie bombing has been the subject of a joint Scottish-US investigation since December 1988.

Mas’ud has been in US custody since 2022. He was originally due to stand trial in May 2025.

That date was set aside following a joint request from the prosecution and defence, who cited the complexity of the case and Mas’ud’s ill health.

The trial was scheduled for this past April, but was called off again after Mas’ud’s legal team asked for more time to prepare.

Judge Friedrich has agreed that the trial’s start date should be pushed back. It is now expected that the trial may not start until next year.
